rationale: Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same M13 Other arthritis phenotype), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), cohorts (UKB), training size (n=174,489), validation size (n=56,192), and both lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so performance metrics cannot differentiate. In this same-publication sibling setting, the best available discriminator is effect size: PGS004547 reports a higher OR per SD (1.262) than PGS004477 (1.196), indicating stronger PRS signal. Method-wise, PGS004547 is a meta/aggregation-style score (RFDiseasemetaPRS), which is a positive structural signal versus a single-score LDpred2 when other fields are matched.

PGS004913 is the better-supported match to the target because it is explicitly disease-focused on alcohol-associated cirrhosis “among heavy drinkers,” with phenotype fields tightly aligned to alcoholic liver cirrhosis and a strong discrimination signal via an extreme-tail effect (OR top vs bottom deciles = 4.4). In contrast, PGS000704 comes from a broad UKB biomarker genetics framework paper (not cirrhosis-focused), reports only a full-model C-index (0.711) that is not PRS-comparable, and its PRS effect size is modest (HR per SD = 1.18), suggesting weaker standalone PRS signal despite the much larger training/validation and genome-wide variant count.

PGS001267 is the better match to the target trait as a generic ankylosing spondylitis diagnosis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both ankylosing spondylitis), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly time-to-event (TTE) framed, which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic disease-risk target. The two candidates are otherwise near-clones (same snpnet method, 10 variants, UKB-only development, identical covariates, same ancestry distribution and validation size), and while PGS001268 has slightly higher PRS-only AUROC/R2 (0.7346/0.1023 vs 0.7265/0.0988), that small metric edge is not enough to outweigh the cleaner endpoint alignment of PGS001267. Both have plausible PRS-only R2 well below the liability h2 ceiling, so heritability does not differentiate.

PGS001344 has cleaner, directly comparable PRS-only performance reported for asthma (PGS-only AUROC=0.64568 and PGS-only R2=0.05973 with basic covariates listed separately), whereas PGS001782 lacks a PRS-only AUROC (only a covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.048844 and a full-model AUROC=0.659 that is not PRS-comparable). Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, but PGS001344’s phenotyping is explicitly “doctor-diagnosed asthma,” and it also shows broader evaluation ancestries (incl. AFR/EAS/SAS) even though the selected metric is EUR. Both come from framework-style papers; given that, the stronger PRS-comparable metrics and clearer PRS-only reporting favor PGS001344 over PGS001782.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable PRS metrics. Candidate_a (PGS005168) is heavily packaged with the CHARGE-AF clinical risk calculator in covariates, making its very high full-model C-index (0.8718) likely covariate-driven and discounted for standalone PRS quality; it does report a strong HR per SD (1.666). Candidate_b (PGS005313) uses much cleaner covariates (age, sex only), has a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.82), and is built with PRS-CSx with substantially more variants (1,271,239 vs 382,963), plus a more diverse evaluation setting (MAE 100% with multiple ancestries listed). Given the reduced leakage risk and stronger effect-size/structural signals, PGS005313 is better-supported for external PRS performance.

PGS002738 is the better match to the target trait (alcohol dependence) on endpoint fidelity: both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are explicitly “Alcohol use disorder,” and trait_efo maps directly to “alcohol dependence,” whereas PGS000201 is framed as “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo “alcohol dependence measurement,” which is a weaker/measurement-oriented alignment. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance must lean on other evidence: PGS002738 shows a stronger risk-gradient effect size (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.96) than the modest ΔR²=0.01192 reported for PGS000201, and it is developed across multiple cohorts (MVP + UKB) rather than UKB-only, supporting robustness. Although PGS000201 has clearly specified basic covariates (a mild positive) and more variants, the combination of tighter endpoint match and stronger effect-size evidence favors PGS002738.

PGS004587 is the better-supported choice for the generic target trait atopic eczema because its endpoint is a direct, general disease incidence phenotype ("Incident atopic dermatitis") aligned to atopic eczema in EUR evaluation, whereas PGS001773 targets a narrower subtype ("Moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis") and is developed/evaluated in a mixed-ancestry Canadian cohort context (MAE) that is less directly comparable to the EUR heritability reference. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R²; PGS001773’s very high reported AUROC/R² are full-model metrics (not PRS-comparable) and are further confounded by inclusion of parental ethnicity covariates, so they should not drive ranking. With comparable lack of PRS-only metrics, PGS004587’s cleaner disease-level endpoint fidelity and simpler non-family-history covariate set outweigh PGS001773’s non-comparable full-model performance claims.

Both candidates have identical endpoint alignment (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported = Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo = alcohol dependence) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so selection rests on structural signals and effect-size evidence. PGS002738 is a genome-wide PRS-CS score with very large variant count (326,000) and shows a slightly stronger discrimination proxy (OR top 10% vs rest 1.96 [1.54–2.51]) than PGS002739 (1.76 [1.32–2.34]). PGS002739 is a very sparse gene-based PRS-CSx model (858 variants) evaluated only in AFR; while ancestry-matched evaluation is a plus for AFR deployment, the sparse construction and weaker OR make it less likely to rank higher in a general benchmark absent PRS-only metrics. Therefore PGS002738 is better-supported overall.

PGS001262 is better-supported for generic angina pectoris risk because it uses a direct doctor-diagnosed angina phenotype (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported align to a diagnosis endpoint), whereas PGS001261 is explicitly time-to-event (TTE), which is a mild endpoint mismatch/packaging risk for a generic disease target. They are otherwise near-clones (same snpnet framework paper, same covariates, same ancestry setup), so PRS-only metrics can break the tie: PGS001262 has slightly higher PGS-only AUROC (0.5868 vs 0.5823) and PGS-only R2 (0.01304 vs 0.01228), both plausible under the heritability ceiling. PGS001261 has larger training N and more variants, but within this same-study sibling comparison those advantages are outweighed by the more target-faithful endpoint and marginally better PRS-only performance of PGS001262.

Both candidates are near-clones for endpoint fidelity and study context (same AAA trait_reported/efo/phenotyping_reported, same PRS-CS method, same variant count, same GWAS ancestry mix and EUR-only evaluation, same Nat Genet publication family). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model metrics are only weakly informative and covariate comparability matters. PGS003973 has explicitly basic covariates (Age, Age^2, Sex) and reports a higher discrimination metric (C-index 0.882 with CI) in that light-adjusted setting, whereas PGS003972 has covariates listed as Unknown and a lower AUROC (0.69). With no PRS-only metrics to separate them, the cleaner disclosed covariate set plus stronger reported discrimination favors PGS003973.

PGS001135 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports clean PGS-only AUROC=0.539 and PGS-only R²=0.00291 (with CI for AUROC) under basic covariates, and these values are plausible under the provided heritability ceiling guidance. PGS004477 has a more genome-wide method/variant count (LDpred2; ~1.06M variants) and a larger EUR validation sample, but it provides no AUC/R² at all and only a modest OR=1.20 with unknown covariates, plus its publication framing (“integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”) raises packaging/comparability uncertainty. Both are UKB-derived EUR models with broadly similar arthritis endpoints, so the decisive difference is that PGS001135 has directly comparable PRS-only performance while PGS004477 lacks comparable metrics and has more ambiguity about what was evaluated.

Both candidates come from the same Nat Genet study, use the same method (PRS-CS), have essentially identical variant counts (~1.11M), identical EUR-only DEV/EVAL ancestry, identical covariates (age, age^2, sex, PCs), identical validation sample size (n=244,450), and both evaluate the same endpoint in practice (phenotyping_reported: incident aortic stenosis). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the main differentiators are endpoint fidelity and effect-size strength: PGS005254 is explicitly an aortic stenosis score (trait_reported/trait_efo match the target) and shows a stronger HR per SD (1.64 vs 1.53 for PGS005255). PGS005255 is framed as a related measurement (mean pressure gradient) with a broader/mixed EFO mapping, so it is slightly less directly aligned to the target trait despite the same incident AS evaluation.

PGS005048 is better-supported for angina pectoris because it uses a direct diagnosis-style endpoint (PheCode 411.3; phenotyping_reported: Angina pectoris) and comes from a disease-focused multi-population PRS methods paper with MVP development, plus it reports a strong PRS effect size (OR per SD 1.487, near the ≥1.5 “strong” guideline). In contrast, PGS001261 is a UKB pan-trait sparse-framework ("across 813 traits") time-to-event phenotype, a known archetype that generalizes less well, and its PRS-only metrics are modest (PGS-only AUROC 0.582; PGS-only R2 0.0123—only slightly above the local h2_obs ceiling scale and indicating weak standalone signal). Although PGS001261 has clean PRS-only AUROC/R2, the combination of framework/TTE endpoint and weak discrimination makes it less likely to rank highly than the MVP-based, diagnosis-anchored score with supportive OR evidence.

PGS002089 has better endpoint fidelity to the target (phenotyping_reported is direct “Ankylosing spondylitis”), whereas PGS001268 is explicitly a time-to-event (TTE) endpoint (“Ankylosing spondylitis (time-to-event)”), which is a known mismatch risk for a generic disease-risk target. Although PGS001268 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.7346; PGS R2 0.10232, below the h2_liability ceiling) and a larger validation sample, it comes from a pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet with only 10 variants), which is a strong generalization warning signal versus PGS002089’s genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2 with 22,026 variants) and explicit multi-ancestry evaluation (EUR/GME/SAS). PGS002089 lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2, but its stronger method/coverage and more deployment-faithful phenotype outweigh the framework+sparse+TTE concerns for PGS001268.

PGS002755 is better supported for the generic target trait (atopic eczema) because its endpoint is a direct disease diagnosis (“Incident atopic dermatitis”) and it uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants, which is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than PGS001773’s very sparse 25-variant score. PGS001773 reports a very high AUROC (0.93) and R² (0.49), but these are full-model metrics (no PGS-only/incremental metrics) and are paired with covariates including parental ethnicity, making the discrimination evidence non-comparable and likely covariate-driven; the R² also looks implausibly above the eczema heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.071), further discounting it. While PGS002755 lacks PRS-only AUC/R², it provides a PRS-linked effect size (HR high vs low PRS=1.249) in a much larger EUR evaluation (n=337,910) with relatively standard covariates, making it the more reliable choice overall.

Both candidates map to the broad target (trait_efo=arthritis), but PGS004547 is more structurally likely to perform better as a PRS: it uses a meta/ensemble-style approach (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with ~1,059,939 variants, whereas PGS001135 is a sparse pan-trait UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”, snpnet) with only 1,028 variants—an archetype noted to generalize poorly. PGS001135 does provide clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.539, R2 0.00291) and basic covariates, but these indicate very weak PRS signal; its PRS-only R2 is also far below the (liability) heritability ceiling, consistent with limited predictive power. PGS004547 lacks AUC/R2 and has unknown covariates (reducing confidence), but it at least reports a moderate OR=1.26 and has a much more genome-wide model structure, making it the better-supported bet for higher external benchmark ranking despite missing comparable metrics.

PGS004913 is better supported as a standalone PRS for the target endpoint: its phenotyping_reported and trait_reported both directly match alcohol-associated cirrhosis, and it is explicitly constructed as a PRS (PRSice-2) with a larger variant set (20 vs 3) and basic, non-leaky covariates (age/sex/PCs). Its reported PRS signal (top vs bottom decile OR=4.4) is consistent with meaningful discrimination even though PRS-only AUC/R2 are not provided. In contrast, PGS001777 is a very sparse 3-variant “genetic risk score” from a paper that explicitly packages genetics with diabetes prediction; it reports only a full-model AUROC (0.671) with unknown covariates, which is not PRS-comparable and may be covariate-driven, and its phenotyping_reported is narrower/less aligned (“Cirrhosis (males)”).

PGS000704 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for alcoholic liver cirrhosis: it targets the exact endpoint (“Alcoholic cirrhosis” with phenotyping_reported matching) and uses a genome-wide, high-coverage snpnet multi-PRS (183,271 variants) trained at large scale (UKB n=223,327) with large evaluation (n=135,300) and some non-EUR evaluation breadth (EUR/MAE). Although it reports only a full-model C-index (0.711) rather than PRS-only metrics, its covariates are clearly basic (age time-scale, sex, batch, PCs), making the reported discrimination less likely to be heavily clinically packaged. In contrast, PGS001777 is a very sparse 3-variant score with unknown covariates, small validation (n=1,390), and a phenotyping mismatch signal (“Cirrhosis (males)”), making its AUROC (0.671) harder to interpret and less likely to generalize despite a strong top-vs-bottom OR.

PGS002727 is more endpoint-faithful to the target use-case via its explicit phenotyping_reported of “Pediatric asthma” and comes from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study, with supportive effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.57) and very large evaluation support (n=391,820; multi-ancestry evaluation listed). PGS001782 is from a global biobank/framework-style paper and, while it reports a clean PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.048844; AUROC 0.659) with basic covariates, it has only a single EUR evaluation record (n=7,128) and lacks disease-focused endpoint detail beyond generic “Asthma.” Given framework scores often underperform disease-focused models unless they have clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence, the pediatric asthma-specific model is slightly better-supported here, though confidence is low because PGS002727 lacks explicit PRS-only AUC/R2 and reports only full-model metrics.

Both candidates align to angina pectoris, but PGS001262 is a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse snpnet score ("across 813 traits") with modest PRS-only performance (PGS-only AUROC 0.5868; PGS-only R2 0.0130), consistent with weak standalone signal and the known framework/generalization penalty. PGS005048 is built in a disease-focused PRS-methods comparison context using MVP as the development cohort, uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred) with far broader variant coverage (1.29M), and—despite lacking PRS-only AUC/R2—reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.487, near the ≥1.5 strong-signal threshold) with only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs). Given endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both, the combination of disease-focused development + genome-wide model structure + strong OR makes PGS005048 more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the sparse UKB framework score.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.78 in PGS005313 vs 0.74 in PGS002814) are only weakly informative and not directly comparable. Given that, structural and transportability signals dominate: PGS005313 uses a genome-wide cross-ancestry shrinkage approach (PRS-CSx) with ~1.27M variants and multi-ancestry GWAS inputs plus explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation, and it shows a strong per-SD OR (1.82). PGS002814 is a much sparser P+T score (4,520 variants) evaluated only in East Asian samples; its reported Nagelkerke R2=0.14 is a full-model metric and is hard to interpret against the AF heritability ceiling without PRS-only isolation. Overall, PGS005313 is better-supported as a more robust, higher-signal, more portable AF PRS, while PGS002814’s evidence is narrower (EAS-only eval) and methodologically more limited.

PGS005252 is the better-supported match to the target trait (aortic stenosis): its trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are directly aligned to incident aortic stenosis, whereas PGS005255 is framed as “Mean pressure gradient” with an aortic measurement EFO mapping (more proxy-like despite mentioning incident AS). Neither model reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size and design signals; PGS005252 shows a stronger HR per SD (1.92 vs 1.53 for PGS005255), suggesting stronger standalone PRS discrimination. Although PGS005252 reports a high full-model C-index (0.87), it uses many clinical covariates (potentially inflating that metric), but this does not outweigh its clearer endpoint labeling and stronger HR evidence compared with PGS005255’s lighter covariates but weaker HR and more measurement-oriented trait framing. Both are EUR-only; validation size differences are not decisive.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS003972 is better-supported structurally and by study archetype: it is a disease-focused multi-cohort GWAS meta-analysis score using a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.1M variants, which is generally more capable of capturing polygenic signal than the very sparse P+T 29-variant PGS000753. Neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC=0.69 reported for PGS003972 cannot be treated as a PRS-comparable advantage; however, PGS000753’s only quantitative support is a moderate OR=1.37 per SD and it is explicitly for a prevalent endpoint, which is a slightly weaker/generalizability signal than the generic AAA endpoint in PGS003972. Overall, the combination of genome-wide construction and broad disease-consortium development makes PGS003972 more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks than the sparse 29-SNP PGS000753, though confidence is tempered by missing PRS-only metrics and unknown covariates for PGS003972.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo atopic eczema; phenotyping_reported incident atopic dermatitis) and use the same covariates and the same EUR evaluation sample size (n=337,910), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. In this near-clone setting, structural PRS quality signals and effect size break the tie: PGS002755 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants versus PGS004587’s 23 genome-wide significant SNPs, which is more likely to capture polygenic signal for eczema. The reported HR separation is also slightly stronger for PGS002755 (HR high vs low 1.249 vs 1.153). PGS004587’s multi-cohort training list is supportive but not enough to outweigh the much sparser construction and weaker HR given otherwise identical endpoint/covariate/validation context.

Both candidates are well-aligned to the target (trait_reported/trait_efo aortic stenosis; incident aortic stenosis phenotyping; EUR dev/eval) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we rely on effect-size evidence and design signals. PGS005254 is trained on a much larger sample (n=205,483 vs 47,691 for PGS005252) and uses a clean, basic covariate set (age/age^2/sex/PCs), reducing concern that any reported association is driven by extensive clinical adjustment. While PGS005252 shows a higher HR (1.92 vs 1.64), its evaluation is embedded in a much more clinically adjusted model (multiple comorbidities plus BMI/smoking/renal failure) and the only discrimination metric shown is a full-model C-index=0.87, which is not PRS-comparable and likely covariate-inflated. Given the absence of PRS-only metrics for both, the larger, cleaner-trained PRS-CS model (PGS005254) is better-supported for external PRS performance than the covariate-heavy, full-model-metric-reliant PGS005252.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all atrial fibrillation) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUCs are not directly comparable as PRS metrics. PGS005168 is heavily confounded by explicit clinical risk-calculator packaging (covariates include CHARGE-AF), making its very high full-model C-index (0.8718) largely non-informative for standalone PRS quality despite a strong HR per SD (1.67). PGS002814 uses only basic covariates (age, sex, PCs), avoiding that packaging/leakage concern, and shows strong PRS signal via OR per SD ~1.94 plus reported pseudo-R2 (0.14) and AUROC 0.74 in its evaluation setting. Given the domain guidance to strongly penalize named clinical risk calculators and prefer cleaner covariate designs when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS002814 is better-supported for external PRS performance.

PGS002739 is the better-supported match to the target trait alcohol dependence because its endpoint is a direct clinical diagnosis construct (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Alcohol use disorder; trait_efo: alcohol dependence) and it comes from a disease-focused AUD study with multi-cohort development listed (MVP, PGC, UKB) and an AFR evaluation context. It also reports a reasonably strong discriminative effect size (OR top 10% vs rest = 1.76, plus β=0.17), whereas PGS000201 is framed as “Problematic alcohol use” with trait_efo mapped to an alcohol dependence measurement and uses a DSM-5 criteria count (log-transformed), which is a more quantitative/problem-use phenotype rather than dependence/AUD case-control. PGS000201’s only performance signal is a small ΔR²=0.01192 (covariate-adjusted), and both candidates lack clean PRS-only AUC/R², so the stronger endpoint fidelity and effect-size evidence favor PGS002739 despite its unknown covariates and smaller variant count.

Both candidates match the target trait (AAA) well, but PGS003973 is better-supported structurally and by study context: it is a genome-wide PRS-CS score (~1.1M variants) developed in a large multi-cohort AAA GWAS meta-analysis (many contributing cohorts) with EUR evaluation, which is generally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the very sparse P+T score in PGS000753 (29 variants) trained on a smaller stated training set. The only performance number for PGS003973 is a full-model C-index (0.882) with basic covariates (age/age^2/sex), which is not PRS-comparable, but PGS000753 also lacks PRS-only metrics; its moderate OR per SD (1.37) provides some PRS signal yet does not offset the strong methodological/variant-count advantage of PGS003973. PGS000753’s ‘prevalent’ endpoint and mixed-ancestry evaluation string add minor uncertainty rather than a clear advantage.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ankylosing spondylitis) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores, so endpoint fidelity and study archetype do not separate them. PGS001267 has substantially stronger directly PRS-comparable performance evidence (PGS-only AUROC 0.7265 and PGS-only R² 0.0988 in Europeans) with only basic covariates, and its PRS-only R² is plausible under the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability ~0.399). In contrast, PGS002089 reports only a partial correlation (partial-r 0.0919) and no PRS-only AUC/R², making its predictive strength harder to benchmark despite a more polygenic LDpred2 construction (22,026 variants) and smaller validation N. Given the clearer, PRS-isolated metrics and stronger quantified discrimination, PGS001267 is better-supported here.

PGS002727 is from a disease-focused pediatric asthma study and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (985,837) and a strong reported per-SD effect size (OR=1.57), plus explicitly multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS). Although it lacks PRS-only AUROC/R² (only full-model AUROC=0.66, R²=0.04) and covariates are unknown, its endpoint is still a direct asthma diagnosis subtype and the effect size suggests meaningful PRS signal. PGS001344 has clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.6457; PGS-only R²=0.0597, below the asthma h2_liability ceiling) and basic covariates, but it comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”) with a very sparse model (6,139 variants) that domain guidance flags as systematically weaker for external transfer than disease-focused models unless it has clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence. Here, the metric edge is modest and does not clearly outweigh the framework/sparsity penalty, so PGS002727 is better-supported overall for likely benchmark performance.

PGS001263 is the better-supported match to the target trait (atrial flutter) because its endpoint is directly aligned: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported are all specifically “Atrial flutter,” whereas PGS001339 targets a broader composite (“atrial fibrillation and flutter”) and is explicitly time-to-event (phenotyping_reported: “TTE atrial fibrillation and flutter”), which is a mild endpoint-fidelity penalty for a generic atrial flutter target. Both are near-clone siblings from the same UKB pan-trait snpnet framework paper with identical training size, covariates, and validation size, so performance is a legitimate tie-break: PGS001263 has slightly higher PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.61716 vs 0.613; PGS-only R2 0.02517 vs 0.02447), with both remaining plausible under the heritability ceiling sanity check. Given the near-identical design, the direct phenotype match plus marginally stronger PRS-only performance favors PGS001263.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication/study family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training size (n=11,734), same validation size (n=11,322), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC=0.632 is not a differentiator. In this tie-like setting, PGS000454 has slightly stronger supportive performance signals (higher Nagelkerke R² 0.0489 vs 0.0487 and higher top-1% vs rest OR 3.79 vs 3.61) with essentially identical per-SD OR, so it is marginally better-supported than PGS000452.

PGS002786 is the better match to the target trait (bipolar disorder): its trait_reported/trait_efo are exactly bipolar disorder, whereas PGS002787 targets the narrower subtype bipolar I disorder. Both candidates come from the same publication, use the same method (SDPR), similar variant counts, EUR-only GWAS/EVAL, basic covariates (age, PCs1-3), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes; both only show small partial R² values in non-disease phenotyping contexts. PGS002787 has a slightly higher partial R² (0.00275 vs 0.00251), but given the near-clone design and the weak comparability of these full-model partial R² metrics, endpoint fidelity to the target trait is the more reliable differentiator here.

PGS001263 is the better-supported choice for the specific target trait (atrial flutter) because its endpoint is an exact match across trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, whereas PGS002050 targets a broader composite (“atrial fibrillation and flutter”), reducing endpoint fidelity to flutter specifically. PGS001263 also provides clean PRS-comparable performance metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.617 and PGS-only R2=0.025), which are interpretable and pass the heritability sanity check (well below the provided h2_obs ceiling), while PGS002050 reports only partial correlation (partial-r=0.103) and lacks PRS-only AUROC/R2, making cross-model benchmarking less direct. Although PGS002050 has a stronger structural setup (LDpred2 with ~555k variants and larger training n) and similarly multi-ancestry evaluation, the absence of PRS-comparable metrics plus the broader phenotype makes it less well-supported for atrial flutter than the exact-flutter model with explicit PRS-only performance.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication/family, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and sizes, same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). In this same-context tie, PGS000454 has slightly better full-model discrimination and fit (AUROC 0.632 vs 0.630; Nagelkerke R² 0.0489 vs 0.0456) and a marginally higher per-SD OR (1.661 vs 1.633), while PGS000456’s only edge is a slightly higher top-1% vs rest OR (3.95 vs 3.79). Given the overall small differences and lack of PRS-only metrics, the advantage for PGS000454 is modest, hence low confidence.

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/phenotyping (basal cell carcinoma), same publication/study family (Cancer PRSweb), same method (GWAS Hits), same EUR-only training/evaluation, same training (n=11,734; MGI), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation size (n=11,322). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences are only a weak tie-break. On the visible metrics, PGS000452 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.632 vs 0.630) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0487 vs 0.0456), while PGS000456 only edges on OR top 1% vs rest (3.95 vs 3.61) and has marginally more variants (30 vs 28). Given the otherwise identical context and the small differences, PGS000452 is marginally better-supported overall, but the decision is close.

PGS000327 has much stronger endpoint fidelity: trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to autism spectrum disorder, whereas PGS002790’s phenotyping_reported is explicitly different ("Psychiatric behavior (withdrawn)"), indicating a proxy/mismatched endpoint despite the ASD label. PGS000327 also comes from a disease-focused ASD GWAS meta-analysis context with clear training scale (n=28,592) and reports a moderate per-SD effect size (OR=1.33), while PGS002790 lacks training sample information and provides only a small partial R² (0.0055) from a cross-psychiatric/cognition study framing. Covariates are similarly light in both (age/sex/PCs), so PGS004621’s much larger European evaluation (n≈1.15M vs n≈30k) and slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.42 vs 1.32) further support it, while PGS000726’s top-vs-bottom quintile OR (2.26) is harder to benchmark across designs and doesn’t offset the sparse construction.

Both candidates are endpoint-faithful for coronary artery disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all CAD) and use essentially the same LDpred genome-wide construction with similar variant counts (~6.6M) and broadly similar multi-ancestry GWAS inputs. PGS002244 is better-supported for likely external benchmark performance because it comes from a larger, explicitly across-ancestries evaluation setting (EVAL includes AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/SAS with large n=343,676) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.64, 95% CI 1.61–1.67), which is a strong PRS-quality signal when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. PGS000013 does report a PRS-comparable R2=0.04, but its headline AUROC=0.81 is full-model (not PRS-only) and thus not directly comparable; it also lacks effect-size evidence in the visible record. Given similar covariate cleanliness (both basic demographics/PCs/array-type style), the stronger effect-size evidence plus broader evaluation context favors PGS002244.

Both candidates match the target trait well (all-cause dementia; EFO dementia). However, PGS005170 is better-supported as a transferable PRS: it is an explicit multi-score integrative/ensemble PRS (24 component PRSs; >1.3M variants), reports a PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.25, giving at least some PRS-specific signal), and is evaluated across multiple ancestries (including non-EUR) rather than only EUR. PGS004281 is a single-biobank UKB-only GenoBoost model with a very small variant set (110) and only full-model metrics (AUROC ~0.819, pseudo-R2 ~0.034) that are not PRS-only; with no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes, its apparent performance is hard to attribute to the PRS itself. Given the domain guidance favoring disease-focused, externally oriented multi-cohort/robust designs and multi-score aggregation when PRS-only metrics are absent, PGS005170 is the stronger pick despite its smaller stated training n and lower full-model AUROC.

PGS004951 is better aligned to the target trait as a generic dilated cardiomyopathy PRS (phenotyping_reported: “Clinical dilated cardiomyopathy”), whereas PGS004949 is explicitly restricted to “Non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy,” a subtype mismatch for the broader target. Both are near-clones from the same Nat Genet study using PRS-CS with similar PRS-only AUC (~0.67–0.68) and similar per-SD OR (~1.9), so performance does not clearly separate them; PGS004949’s larger validation N and slightly higher PRS-only AUC are offset by heavier covariate adjustment (age, age^2, array) and the subtype-specific endpoint. Given endpoint fidelity is the top-ranked selection factor, PGS004951 is the stronger choice.

PGS002036 is the better-supported choice for the target trait depressive disorder because it has cleaner trait alignment (trait_efo exactly matches “depressive disorder” vs PGS004760 mapped to “major depressive disorder”) and substantially stronger transportability evidence: it is evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS) rather than EUR-only. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be compared directly; PGS004760’s only metric is an incremental/full-model R2=0.024 (covariate-adjusted) which is not a clean PRS-comparable signal. Given similar basic covariates, PGS002036’s broader evaluation context and closer endpoint mapping outweigh PGS004760’s larger variant count and newer method label.

PGS004281 is the better-supported match to the target trait dementia on endpoint fidelity: it is explicitly "All-cause dementia" for both trait_reported and phenotyping_reported and maps to the dementia EFO, whereas PGS000823 is labeled "Alzheimer's disease" (trait_efo Alzheimer disease) despite phenotyping_reported being incident all-cause dementia, creating a concept/endpoint mismatch for a generic dementia target. Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so PGS004281’s reported full-model AUROC (~0.819) cannot be treated as PRS performance but is at least based on basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) without obvious leakage; PGS000823 provides only a modest HR (1.36 top vs bottom tertile) and uses a sparse 23-variant GWS score. Structurally, PGS004281’s larger-variant, genome-wide method (110 variants, GenoBoost) and large UKB development/validation context make it more likely to rank higher for all-cause dementia than the older, very sparse AD-focused score.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to coronary artery disease (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all CAD) and only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs; PGS000013 also adds chip), so phenotype/covariate comparability is not a differentiator. PGS003725 is better-supported for likely external benchmark performance because it comes from a clearly disease-focused, modern multi-ancestry CAD PRS study with broad multi-ancestry evaluation (EVAL spans AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/MAE/SAS) and reports strong PRS effect sizes (HR 1.75 and OR 2.14 per SD), which is strong discrimination evidence even without AUC/R2. PGS000013 provides a PRS-only R2=0.04 (below the CAD heritability ceiling, so plausible), but its strongest visible AUROC (0.81) is full-model and not PRS-comparable, and it lacks effect-size evidence here; overall it looks more like an older general common-disease score with less direct multi-ancestry robustness evidence than PGS003725.

Both candidates target the same trait framing (“Dilated cardiomyopathy (MTAG)”) and use the same method (PRS-CS) with only basic demographic/PC covariates, so performance/evidence fields can reasonably differentiate them. PGS004949 provides PRS-comparable metrics (explicit univariate PRS-only AUC=0.68 with CI and delta PRS/residual R² on the liability scale=0.095), plus a slightly stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.91 vs 1.76 for PGS004862). PGS004862 lacks any PRS-only AUC/R² and reports only full-model AUROC=0.71/R²=0.05, which is not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Although PGS004862 has cleaner EUR-only evaluation and slightly larger validation N, PGS004949’s direct PRS-only performance reporting and stronger effect size make it better-supported for ranking.

PGS000997 is better-supported on PRS-comparable evidence: it reports explicit PGS-only AUROC=0.591 and PGS-only R²=0.0178 (no covariates), with basic covariates listed and a heritability-sane magnitude (below the ~0.02 local h2_obs match for ICD10 K57). It also has broader evaluation ancestry coverage (EUR plus AFR/EAS/SAS) and clear phenotype description (TTE diverticular disease of intestine). In contrast, PGS004544 has an exact ICD10 K57 endpoint and a moderate OR=1.32, but provides no AUC/R², unknown covariates, and comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framing that can reflect packaging rather than standalone PRS performance; with missing comparable metrics, it is less directly supported for benchmark ranking despite larger variant count and validation N.

PGS002036 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (depressive disorder) because its endpoint alignment is cleaner (trait_efo exactly matches depressive disorder; phenotyping_reported is simply “Depression”), whereas PGS003578 is explicitly framed as lifetime Major Depressive Disorder with trait_efo mapped to major depressive disorder (a narrower/different EFO concept than the target). Neither candidate provides PRS-only AUC/R², so performance evidence cannot strongly differentiate; PGS003578’s reported R²=0.0257 appears to be a full-model/unspecified R² (not labeled PRS-only) and thus is not a reliable advantage. Both are UKB-based and multi-ancestry evaluated, but PGS002036 comes from a portability framework paper (a known weakness) while PGS003578 is also UKB-centric; with metrics largely non-comparable, the decisive visible edge is PGS002036’s closer trait/EFO match to the target.

PGS005170 is better aligned to the target trait dementia (trait_reported = all-cause dementia; phenotyping_reported = incident all-cause dementia; trait_efo = dementia), whereas PGS000823 is primarily framed as Alzheimer’s disease (trait_reported/trait_efo = Alzheimer’s disease) despite using an incident all-cause dementia phenotype. Structurally, PGS005170 uses an integrative ensemble of 24 component PRSs with genome-wide methods and ~1.32M variants, which is a strong positive signal versus PGS000823’s 23 genome-wide significant variants. On performance evidence, neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; PGS005170 at least provides an HR per SD (1.25) plus a full-model AUROC (0.761) with mostly standard covariates aside from APOE dosage, while PGS000823 provides only a tertile HR (1.36 top vs bottom) and minimal covariates, making direct PRS strength harder to gauge. Although PGS000823 has a larger validation sample (12,978 vs 2,032), validation N is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh PGS005170’s stronger endpoint fidelity to dementia and stronger methodological/variant-coverage signals.

PGS004614 is from a disease-focused diverticular disease GWAS/prediction study (Cell Genom) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (SBayesR) with very large variant coverage (1,082,282) and some multi-ancestry evaluation listed, which is structurally and archetypically more likely to transfer than a sparse pan-trait UKB framework score. PGS000997, while it reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.591, R2 0.0178) and has large UKB training/validation, is explicitly from the “813 traits in UK Biobank” snpnet framework that domain guidance flags as systematically underperforming disease-focused models; its PRS-only performance is modest and its endpoint is time-to-event, adding mismatch risk for a generic diverticular disease target. PGS004614’s reported AUROC (0.76) is full-model and includes family history (covariate leakage), so it can’t be used as PRS-only evidence, but the overall disease-specific study context + genome-wide method/coverage outweighs the framework penalty on PGS000997.

PGS004614 is the better-supported diverticular disease PRS because it is clearly disease-focused (publication explicitly on diverticular disease risk variants) and uses a strong genome-wide shrinkage method (SBayesR) with broad multi-ancestry evaluation listed (AFR/EUR/SAS), suggesting more robustness than a EUR-only evaluation. Although its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC=0.76 and it includes family history (making that AUROC non-PRS-comparable), PGS004544 provides even less directly comparable performance evidence (no AUC/R2 at all) and appears to be a risk-factor metaPRS integration framework (RFDiseasemetaPRS) rather than a direct disease-GWAS-derived score; its lone OR=1.32 per SD is only moderate. With both lacking PRS-only metrics, the disease-focused study archetype plus stronger method/transportability context favors PGS004614 over PGS004544.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported/phenotyped endpoint (“Nodular lymphoma” mapped to follicular lymphoma), same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI) and size (n=3,696), same validation size (n=3,256), and same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; full-model AUROC differences are small and likely noise. In this tie-like setting, PGS000644 has slightly stronger overall discrimination/effect evidence (full-model AUROC 0.538 vs 0.532; per-SD OR 1.149 vs 1.133; higher Nagelkerke R² 0.00349 vs 0.00282) and a larger variant set (2.21M vs 1.05M), so it is marginally better-supported than PGS000643 despite PGS000643’s higher top-1% vs rest OR.

PGS002304 has the cleanest endpoint fidelity to the target: trait_reported and phenotyping_reported are both explicitly “Follicular lymphoma,” matching the target directly, whereas PGS000643 is labeled/phenotyped as “Nodular lymphoma” (despite trait_efo mapping to follicular lymphoma), introducing ambiguity in the actual evaluated endpoint. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values are only weakly comparable; still, PGS002304 shows higher reported AUROC (0.61 vs 0.532). Although PGS000643 has a stronger genome-wide method (PRS-CS, ~1.0M variants) and reports PRS effect sizes, the endpoint mismatch risk plus weaker discrimination evidence makes PGS002304 the better-supported choice for follicular lymphoma overall.

PGS000644 is better-supported as a standalone PRS for follicular lymphoma because it is a genome-wide lassosum score with ~2.2M variants and reports PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD 1.149, plus pseudo-R²=0.00349), with clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch) and a much larger European evaluation sample (n=3,256). PGS002304 has perfect endpoint fidelity (follicular lymphoma) but is a very sparse 6-variant GWAS-hits score with unknown covariates and only a full-model AUROC (0.61) that is not PRS-comparable; its evaluation is also very small (n=197), making the apparent AUROC advantage hard to trust for PRS ranking. Despite PGS000644’s label mismatch (“Nodular lymphoma”), its trait_efo maps to follicular lymphoma and the overall evidence package (method/scale + PRS-linked metrics) is stronger.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to Dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and direct diagnosis phenotyping). However, PGS001254 comes from the known pan-trait UKB sparse-PRS framework (“across 813 traits”) with an extremely sparse 11-variant snpnet model, which is a warning sign for external generalization despite reporting clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.665/0.0247) in EUR only. PGS002092, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R², is a genome-wide LDpred2 score with ~484k variants and is explicitly evaluated across multiple ancestries (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS), a stronger transportability/robustness context than EUR-only evaluation. Given the framework+sparsity penalty on PGS001254 and the stronger structural/portability evidence for PGS002092, PGS002092 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=18,971), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. The main differentiators are (i) slightly higher PRS-comparable performance for PGS002092 (partial-r 0.0797 vs 0.0783 for PGS001880, with very similar CIs) and (ii) stronger structural properties: PGS002092 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (484,484 vs 2,443), which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal when other fields are matched. Given the same study family and essentially identical design, the small partial-r edge plus the more genome-wide construction supports PGS002092 as more likely to rank higher, though confidence is only moderate because the performance difference is small.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity to dupuytren contracture (matching trait_efo and direct diagnosis phenotyping). PGS001254 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6646; PGS-only R² 0.0247), but it comes from the pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse snpnet framework with an extremely small variant set (11), a known pattern that often generalizes poorly outside its narrow setting. PGS001880, while lacking PRS-only AUROC/R², is a genome-wide penalized-regression score with far more variants (2443) and—critically—has explicit multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/GME/SAS) in a portability-focused study, providing stronger visible evidence of transportability/robustness than PGS001254’s EUR-only evaluation. Given the benchmark goal of external performance, the broader evaluation context and less-sparse architecture make PGS001880 better-supported overall despite missing AUC/R².

PGS001792 is better-supported for glaucoma PRS performance because it reports a PRS-comparable metric (Nagelkerke’s R2 with covariates regressed out / PGS-only R2 = 0.03209), which is interpretable as standalone PRS signal and is below the glaucoma heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0556), making it plausible. PGS004944 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only a full-model AUROC (0.748) plus an OR=1.74, but its endpoint is explicitly self-reported POAG and its AUROC is not PRS-comparable; thus its evidence is less directly comparable. Both have acceptable basic covariates, but PGS001792 also has a stronger structural setup (PRS-CS-auto, genome-wide 911k variants) and a clear multi-cohort development context, whereas PGS004944’s training context is not shown and uses a sparser Lassosum score (144k variants).

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported, same method PRSCS, same evaluation ancestry string and validation n=94,651, and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 so full-model AUROC is only a weak tie-break). In this same-publication sibling setting, PGS005271 has consistently stronger visible performance proxies: higher reported AUROC (0.6297 vs 0.6054) and stronger effect sizes (OR per SD 1.55 vs 1.42; beta 0.438 vs 0.349). Variant counts are essentially identical and covariates are unknown for both, so the stronger discrimination/effect-size evidence favors PGS005271.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), come from the same publication, have identical training cohort (UKB), training N (6,704), evaluation ancestry mix (EUR/SAS), covariates listed as 0, and the same validation sample size (90,274), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so this is a near-clone comparison where within-family performance can break the tie. PGS004160 (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) shows consistently stronger reported discrimination/effect evidence than PGS004018 (lassosum.CV): higher full-model AUROC (0.694 vs 0.678), higher R² (0.089 vs 0.073), and higher per-SD OR (2.05 vs 1.93). Given identical context and no covariate-packaging differences, the ensemble MultiPRS structure plus the uniformly better metrics support PGS004160 as more likely to rank higher externally.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication/study family (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=31,804), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). In this same-context tie, PGS005083 has a marginally higher full-model C-index (0.75368 vs 0.75358) and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.455 vs 1.452), so it is weakly better-supported than PGS005077, though the differences are tiny and likely noise.

PGS001792 is better-supported for glaucoma risk prediction because it provides a PRS-comparable metric (pgs_only_r2 / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2 = 0.03209) with basic demographic/PC covariates and a very large evaluation sample (n=347,396), and its endpoint is explicitly primary open-angle glaucoma (a direct glaucoma subtype match). In contrast, PGS000137 is from a disease-focused glaucoma paper but reports only a full-model AUROC (0.8) with family history included as a covariate (making the AUROC less informative for standalone PRS quality) and provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect sizes; its validation sample is also much smaller (n=1,795). While PGS001792 comes from a broader global-biobank framework context, the presence of a clean PRS-only R2 plus large-scale evaluation outweighs PGS000137’s lack of PRS-isolated performance evidence.

PGS002763 has better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is directly “Hip osteoarthritis,” whereas PGS002728 uses “Total hip replacement,” a treatment/proxy endpoint that can introduce non-disease factors (surgical access/indication) and is less aligned to generic hip OA. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either candidate, the full-model AUROC=0.66 in PGS002728 (age, sex adjusted) is not a reliable PRS-comparable differentiator. Structurally, PGS002763 uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS) with ~1.05M variants and shows a moderate per-SD OR=1.38 (1.31–1.46), supporting meaningful PRS signal, while PGS002728 is a sparse 44-variant GWAS-hits score with no effect-size evidence shown. Both are EUR-only evaluation, so ancestry doesn’t separate them; overall the direct phenotype match plus stronger polygenic modeling favors PGS002763.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported = lymphocytic thyroiditis; trait_efo = Hashimoto's thyroiditis), same publication family, same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%) and same validation sample size (n=94,651), with covariates unknown for both—so full-model AUROC differences (0.639 in PGS005270 vs 0.605 in PGS005272) are not reliable for ranking. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the more informative differentiators are structural properties and effect sizes: PGS005272 uses PRSCS with genome-wide coverage (1,085,142 variants) and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.42) than PGS005270’s very weak OR≈1.04 from a 55-variant P+T score. Given the same study/endpoint context, the stronger effect size plus method/variant-count advantage makes PGS005272 better-supported for external performance.

PGS004944 is better supported for the target trait glaucoma because it has tighter endpoint fidelity to the clinically dominant subtype (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both primary open-angle glaucoma/POAG; trait_efo open-angle glaucoma) and provides stronger PRS-specific evidence via an OR per SD of 1.74 (strong discriminative signal) alongside a very large validation sample (n=407,667) and multi-ancestry validation context. In contrast, PGS000137 is broader/less coherent on labeling (trait_reported glaucoma but phenotyping_reported POAG), uses a sparse C+T score with far fewer variants (2,673), has much smaller validation (n=1,795), and its only performance figure is a full-model AUROC=0.8 that is likely inflated/non-comparable given inclusion of self-reported family history as a covariate and absence of PRS-only metrics or effect sizes.

Both candidates are near-clones: same gout endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Gout”), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (6,704), same stated covariates (“0”), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (90,274). With no PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the best available tie-break is within-family empirical performance and effect sizes: PGS004160 shows higher full-model AUROC (0.694 vs 0.685), higher R² (0.089 vs 0.080), and slightly stronger OR per SD (2.05 vs 2.00) than PGS004047. Method-wise, PGS004160 is an ensemble/MultiPRS approach, which is a positive structural signal over a single-score LDpred2 sibling when other fields are matched.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), publication family, evaluation ancestry mix, and identical validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a reliable differentiator). In this no-PRS-only-metrics setting, structural signals and effect sizes matter more: PGS005271 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.55, β≈0.44), consistent with meaningful PRS signal, whereas PGS005270 is a very sparse P+T score (55 variants) with a near-null effect size (OR≈1.04, β≈0.04) despite a slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.639 vs 0.630), a difference likely within noise and potentially covariate-driven. Therefore PGS005271 is better-supported as the stronger standalone PRS.

PGS002763 is the better-supported hip osteoarthritis PRS on the visible fields: it has direct endpoint fidelity (trait_reported and phenotyping_reported both explicitly “Hip osteoarthritis”) and reports a stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.38, 95% CI 1.31–1.46) than PGS004478 (OR≈1.296 with no CI shown). Both candidates lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so effect-size evidence becomes a key differentiator; PGS002763’s higher OR suggests stronger standalone PRS signal. PGS004478 has a larger stated training sample (n=174,489) and slightly larger validation n, but those are weak signals here, and its publication framing (“Integration of risk factor PRS with disease PRS”) plus unknown covariates adds uncertainty about packaging/augmentation, whereas PGS002763 discloses standard basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical) consistent with cleaner PRS evaluation.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported match), same publication and release date, same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=31,804), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and study context indistinguishable, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005083 has a slightly higher full-model C-index (0.75368 vs 0.75325) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.455 vs 1.443). These are marginal, so confidence is low, but they favor PGS005083.

PGS002728 is better-supported for the target (hip osteoarthritis) because it comes from a disease-focused OA risk assessment study with multi-cohort development (8 cohorts listed) and reports an actual discrimination metric in validation (full-model AUROC 0.66 with CI 0.62–0.70, age/sex-adjusted) on a defined endpoint (total hip replacement) that is a clinically specific proxy for severe hip OA. In contrast, PGS004478 is from a broader “risk factor PRS + disease PRS integration” framework, trained only in UKB with covariates unknown, and provides no AUROC/R2 at all—only a single OR=1.296 (moderate/weak signal) with limited performance context. Both are EUR-only and map to the same EFO, but PGS002728 has clearer endpoint/validation evidence and less framework-style packaging risk.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/phenotyping (Hodgkin's disease), same EFO mapping (Hodgkins lymphoma), same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), same training (n=736) and validation size (n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). In this like-for-like setting, PGS000639 shows consistently stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000638: higher full-model AUROC (0.62 vs 0.601), higher pseudo-R² (0.0276 vs 0.0193), higher OR per SD (1.476 vs 1.377), and higher top-1% vs rest OR (2.64 vs 1.62), plus slightly more variants (20 vs 16). Given identical endpoint and evaluation context, these within-family differences favor PGS000639.

Both candidates are near-clones: same CHF PheCode 428.1 endpoint (maps well to heart failure), same EFO, same method (LDpred), identical variant count (1,286,612), same covariates (age/sex/20 PCs), same training cohort (MVP), same ancestry distribution, and same validation size (n=31,804). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2; only full-model C-index is shown, so differences are marginal. As a tie-break within this identical context, PGS005077 has trivially higher full-model C-index (0.75358 vs 0.75325) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.452 vs 1.443), so it is marginally better-supported than PGS005076.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Hodgkin's disease”), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), cohorts (MGI), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and validation size (n=775), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics). In this same-study, same-endpoint setting, the small full-model performance differences are one of the few differentiators: PGS000638 shows slightly higher AUROC (0.601 vs 0.574) and higher pseudo-R² (0.0193 vs 0.013) and a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.377 vs 1.30). Although PGS000637 uses a genome-wide PRS-CS model with many variants, the observed validation metrics here favor PGS000638, so it is marginally better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones: same Graves’ disease endpoint (a strong match to hyperthyroidism), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix (MAE 100%), same validation N (94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC reported with unknown covariates). With endpoint and study context essentially identical, the only differentiators are small performance/effect-size differences: PGS005265 has slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.6652 vs 0.6637) and stronger per-SD effect sizes (OR 1.625 vs 1.543; β 0.486 vs 0.434). These are modest and likely noisy, hence low confidence, but they favor PGS005265.

PGS004234 is from a hypertension-focused, explicitly multi-ethnic study with multi-cohort development (BioMe + UKB) and multi-ancestry validation (European, African American/Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, Asian), which is supportive for real-world transportability to a generic hypertension target. Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC=0.763 with many non-genetic covariates including BMI and smoking), PGS001320’s clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC=0.629, R2=0.0649) come from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet) with EUR-only development and European-selected performance, a study archetype that domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable in external validation than disease-focused multi-cohort scores. Given the framework penalty and narrower development context for PGS001320 versus the disease-focused multi-ancestry design of PGS004234, PGS004234 is better-supported overall despite weaker directly comparable PRS-only metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported trait/phenotyping (Hodgkin's disease), same EFO mapping (Hodgkins lymphoma), same publication (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (MGI), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), and same validation sample size (n=775). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on within-family performance/effect-size evidence. PGS000639 shows consistently stronger discrimination and association than PGS000637 in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.62 vs 0.574; Nagelkerke R² 0.0276 vs 0.013; per-SD OR 1.476 vs 1.30; top 1% OR 2.64 vs 1.67), with comparable covariate adjustment, making it better-supported for higher external ranking despite having far fewer variants (20 vs 1,047,511).

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Commun paper with the same reported trait/EFO (hypertension), identical phenotyping_reported (prevalent hypertension), identical covariates (age/sex/PCs plus smoking and BMI), same training N (10,314) and same validation size (39,035) with MAE evaluation—so full-model AUROC 0.764 vs 0.763 is essentially noise and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2. In this tie context, PGS004236 has stronger supportive evidence: it reports a substantial PRS effect size (OR=2.1, 95% CI 1.99–2.21) while PGS004234 reports no effect sizes, and it uses a multi-score aggregation-style method (PRSsum) with a larger variant set (398,805 vs 234,228), both of which are positive structural signals when endpoints and covariates are matched.

Both candidates are near-clones: same gout endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all gout), same publication, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (6,704), same evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (90,274), and both list covariates as 0 with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (so full-model AUROC/R² are only weak tie-breakers). In this same-context comparison, PGS004047 shows consistently stronger reported performance/effect-size signals than PGS004018: higher full-model AUROC (0.685 vs 0.678), higher R² (0.0801 vs 0.0734), and higher per-SD OR (1.999 vs 1.927). With endpoints and study context matched, these modest but consistent advantages favor PGS004047.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical trait/phenotyping ("Disorders of iron metabolism"), identical training size (n=391,124), identical covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), and identical ancestry distribution and validation size (n=19,883), so endpoint fidelity and study context do not differentiate them. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the best available comparable metric is the selected European partial correlation, where PGS002031 is slightly higher (partial-r 0.1355 vs 0.1307 for PGS001823). Structurally, PGS002031 also uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with many more variants (6,713 vs 654), which is a supportive tie-break in this same-publication setting.

PGS005266 is a disease-focused, multi-cohort biobank meta-analysis score for Graves’ disease (a clinically dominant cause of hyperthyroidism) with very large genome-wide coverage (1,085,170 variants; PRSCS) and multi-ancestry evaluation context (African American/LatAm/European listed), plus a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.54), which is supportive of meaningful PRS discrimination even though only a full-model AUROC is shown. PGS001043 is an exact-label hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis score but comes from the known pan-trait UKB “813 traits” sparse framework (snpnet, 69 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically weaker for external transfer; its PRS-only metrics are modest (PGS-only AUROC 0.6323; R2 0.0216, below the heritability ceiling but not strong). Given the framework penalty and extreme sparsity of PGS001043 versus the disease-focused, genome-wide PRSCS construction and strong OR for PGS005266, PGS005266 is more likely to rank higher in real-world benchmark performance despite missing PRS-only AUROC/R2.

PGS000114 is the better-supported match to the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint is the umbrella JIA diagnosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to JIA), whereas PGS000325 is explicitly for the oligoarticular subtype (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are subtype-specific), which is a phenotype mismatch for a generic JIA benchmark. Both candidates come from the same disease-focused publication, use the same method (SparSNP), same basic covariates (sex, PCs 1–10), and EUR-only development/evaluation, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so the higher full-model AUROC for PGS000325 (0.80 vs 0.738) is discounted and not decisive. With endpoint fidelity prioritized and other design signals largely near-clone, PGS000114 is more likely to transfer to a generic JIA evaluation setting.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Nat Genet study with identical endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; trait_efo matches), same method (PRS-CS), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), same development cohorts, and same validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are not directly PRS-comparable). In this same-context comparison, PGS004911 has the stronger overall performance/effect-size evidence: higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.73), higher R² (0.048 vs 0.031), and slightly stronger effect sizes (HR 2.34 vs 1.97; OR per SD 1.33 vs 1.26; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9 vs 5.5). Additionally, its trait_reported indicates an MTAG-enhanced HCM score, which domain guidance mildly prefers over the base variant when all else is equal.

Both candidates are near-clone siblings from the same disease-focused paper (same method SparSNP, EUR-only dev/eval, same covariates sex+PCs, similar training/validation sizes), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—only full-model AUROC plus per-SD OR. In this same-context comparison, PGS000325 shows materially stronger performance evidence than PGS000326: higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.76) and notably higher OR per SD (1.93 vs 1.51), while variant count is also higher (21 vs 12). Endpoint-wise both are JIA subtypes; neither is a perfect match to the umbrella target, so the stronger discrimination/effect-size package in PGS000325 is the better-supported pick.

PGS004236 is better-supported for real-world hypertension PRS use because it comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort, explicitly multi-ethnic study (BioMe/MVP/UKB) with multi-ancestry evaluation and a strong reported PRS association (OR=2.1 per SD), whereas PGS001320 is a pan-trait UKB framework score (“across 813 traits”) using a sparse snpnet model that domain guidance flags as systematically less transferable. Although PGS001320 reports clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC=0.629, PGS R2=0.0649) and these are plausible under the hypertension heritability ceiling, its evidence is primarily internal UKB EUR validation and the framework archetype is a major negative signal versus the targeted multi-cohort design of PGS004236. PGS004236’s reported AUROC (0.764) is full-model with heavier covariates (incl. BMI/smoking) and thus not directly comparable, but the combination of endpoint fidelity (prevalent hypertension), multi-cohort development, and strong effect size outweighs the framework metric advantage of PGS001320.

PGS005265 is better-supported for the target hyperthyroidism because its endpoint (Graves’ disease; phenotyping_reported: graves’ disease) is a clinically dominant and tightly aligned subtype of hyperthyroidism, and it comes from a disease-focused, multi-biobank study with broad external evaluation ancestry (African American/Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic/Latin American, European) and a large validation sample (n=94,651). Although it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 (only a full-model AUROC=0.665 is shown), it provides strong PRS-relevant effect-size evidence (OR per SD ≈1.63), which is a meaningful discriminator signal. In contrast, PGS001043 has an exact-label match (hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis) and clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC=0.6323; R2=0.0216, below the heritability ceiling), but it is from the known pan-trait UKB ‘813 traits’ sparse snpnet framework with very few variants (69) and single-biobank development, which domain guidance flags as systematically less transferable than disease-focused multi-cohort scores. Net: the framework penalty and sparse architecture outweigh PGS001043’s modest PRS-only AUROC advantage.

PGS004911 is better-supported as a standalone HCM PRS: it targets the same endpoint (phenotyping_reported: hypertrophic cardiomyopathy) but uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant count (374,114) and reports PRS-linked effect sizes (HR 2.34; OR per SD 1.33; high-vs-median tertile OR 5.9) under only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), which is more comparable to PRS performance. PGS000739 is a sparse 27-variant GWS score and its reported AUROC (0.821) is from a covariate-heavy model including multiple clinical risk factors plus rare-variant carrier status, making the full-model AUROC less informative about PRS contribution and more prone to clinical packaging/leakage. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the cleaner covariate design and stronger genome-wide construction favor PGS004911 despite PGS000739’s multi-ancestry evaluation.

PGS005218 is better-supported as a hypothyroidism PRS candidate because it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with explicit incident hypothyroidism phenotyping and broad multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.) plus a very large European evaluation sample (n=441,692). Although its only reported discrimination is a full-model AUROC (0.859) that is heavily covariate-inflated by thyroid biomarkers (TSH, T4, anti-TPO) and thus not PRS-comparable, PGS002766 provides even less direct performance support (no AUC/R2 at all, only OR=1.47 per SD) and is from a cross-disease family-history comparison framework with unclear training sample size (N/A) and a smaller evaluation (n=39,444). With both lacking PRS-only metrics, the stronger endpoint-specific, multi-cohort disease study context and larger evaluation support favor PGS005218.

PGS000114 is the better-supported choice for the target trait (juvenile idiopathic arthritis) because its endpoint fidelity matches the umbrella disease directly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all JIA), whereas PGS000326 is explicitly a subtype score (RF-negative polyarticular JIA) with a different EFO and phenotyping. Both are from the same publication, same method (SparSNP), same EUR-only dev/eval ancestry, and similarly basic covariates (sex, PCs 1-10), so the main differentiator is phenotype alignment; additionally, PGS000114 shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 2.085 vs 1.51), while the small full-model AUROC difference (0.738 vs 0.76) is not decisive given neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported/phenotyped trait (N18 chronic renal failure) mapped to kidney failure, same publication, same EUR-only DEV/EVAL, same UKB training cohort, identical variant count, and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either. With metrics absent, the main differentiator is the available effect-size evidence: PGS004562 reports a materially stronger per-SD OR (1.395) than PGS004492 (1.171), suggesting stronger standalone PRS signal in the same validation setting. Method differences (metaPRS vs LDpred2) are secondary here given identical endpoint/context and lack of comparable PRS-only metrics.

PGS004908 is better-supported for the target trait (kidney cancer) because it comes from a kidney-cancer–focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis and shows materially stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR=1.5 per SD) with a much richer variant set (107 SNPs) than PGS000076 (19 SNPs; HR=1.16 per SD, suggesting weak-to-moderate discrimination). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and only report full-model AUROC (0.74 vs 0.722), so the small AUROC difference is not decisive; in that setting, the stronger effect size and more substantial disease-specific GWAS-hit construction favor PGS004908. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (PGS000076 is RCC/incident kidney cancer; RCC is a dominant subtype), but PGS000076 is from a cross-cancer evaluation framework and does not compensate with stronger PRS-specific metrics.

PGS004562 is better aligned to the generic target of kidney failure via a direct diagnosis-code endpoint (phenotyping_reported/trait_reported: N18 chronic renal failure) and shows a stronger PRS effect size (OR=1.395 per SD) than PGS000708’s more modest HR=1.19. PGS000708 also has an endpoint restriction (“Diabetic kidney failure in all”), making it a narrower subtype that may transfer worse to a general kidney failure benchmark; its only discrimination metric is a full-model C-index=0.779 (not PRS-only) and thus not a clean PRS comparator. However, both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and both are UKB EUR-only, while PGS004562 has unknown covariates and a framework-like ‘risk factor + disease metaPRS’ design that could imply packaging/leakage—so the win is based mainly on endpoint generality and stronger OR, hence low confidence.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypothyroidism) and are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated in UKB, and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2. Candidate_a (PGS004935) reports only a full-model AUROC=0.70 (not PRS-comparable) with unknown covariates and a smaller evaluation sample (n=8,417), so its apparent performance is hard to interpret for standalone PRS quality. Candidate_b (PGS002766) has a clearer, basic covariate set (age, sex, PCs, technical covariates) and a much more genome-wide PRS construction (PRS-CS with 1,092,122 variants vs 6,127), plus a slightly stronger-supported evaluation context (n=39,444) and a very similar per-SD OR (1.47 vs 1.50). With no PRS-only metrics available, the stronger structural method/variant coverage and cleaner covariate transparency make PGS002766 the better-supported choice.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and evaluation context: same trait_reported/trait_efo (kidney cancer / renal cell carcinoma), same phenotyping_reported (incident kidney cancer), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, same covariates, same cohort lists, and same validation sample size (n=391,610). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R²; the visible AUROC/C-index are full-model and essentially identical (AUROC 0.722; C-index 0.724 vs 0.723). The only substantive difference is that PGS000787 is explicitly derived from PGS000076 but with inverse variant weights, and it shows slightly weaker HR (1.15 vs 1.16) with no compensating PRS-only metric advantage; its reported R²=0.366 is a full-model/unspecified R² and is not PRS-comparable (and would be implausible vs the low heritability ceiling if interpreted as PRS-only). Given the same-context tie-break, the original GWAS-hits score PGS000076 is marginally better supported than the inverted-weights derivative.

Both candidates are near-clones: same late-onset Alzheimer’s disease endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo) and same phenotyping_reported (familial LOAD), same method (genome-wide significant variants) and variant count (21), same publication and covariates (age, sex), and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2. With endpoint and design essentially identical, the main differentiators are (i) effect size and (ii) transportability context. PGS000054 shows a materially stronger per-SD odds ratio (OR=1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93) than PGS000053 (OR=1.29, 1.21–1.37), which is a strong signal of better PRS discrimination when AUC/R2 are absent. Although PGS000053 has a larger EUR validation sample (n=4,792 vs 3,324) and EUR-on-EUR evaluation, validation N is a weak tie-break and does not outweigh the much stronger OR evidence. Therefore PGS000054 is better-supported as the higher-performing PRS for the target trait.

PGS004908 is better-supported as a standalone kidney-cancer PRS: it is derived from a dedicated, disease-focused multi-ancestry GWAS meta-analysis (Nat Genet) and uses a substantially richer GWAS-hit set (107 variants) with a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.5, 95% CI 1.43–1.58), which is a key proxy for PRS discriminative power when PRS-only AUC/R2 are absent. PGS000787 is a pan-cancer risk-factor integration study and the score is explicitly a small 19-variant reuse/inversion of another PGS (PGS000076), with only modest PRS signal (HR=1.15, 1.07–1.24) and incident-only framing; its reported AUROC/R² are full-model and likely covariate-driven, so they don’t provide clean PRS-comparable evidence. Both are EUR-evaluated and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger disease-focused provenance plus materially stronger effect size favors PGS004908.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R². The key differentiator is that PGS000054 provides a strong PRS-relevant effect size (OR per SD 1.73, 95% CI 1.57–1.93), which is meaningful discrimination evidence, while PGS000334 provides only an R²=0.191 that appears to be a full-model/unspecified metric (listed under other_metrics with unknown covariates) and is also suspiciously high relative to the provided EUR heritability ceiling (h2_obs≈0.0084; h2_liability≈0.0269), reducing its interpretability. PGS000054 also has explicitly basic covariates (age, sex) and broad multi-cohort disease-focused development, whereas PGS000334 has unknown covariates and a simpler C+T construction with similarly small variant count. Overall, PGS000054 is better-supported by comparable, PRS-relevant evidence.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported/trait_efo are knee osteoarthritis). However, PGS002729’s only performance evidence is a full-model AUROC=0.66 with covariates including BMI (not PRS-comparable and potentially covariate-driven), and it provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 or effect-size signal.
