PGS002767 also lacks PRS-only AUC/R2, but it reports a clear PRS effect size (OR per SD=1.35, 95% CI 1.30–1.40) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS; ~1.05M variants), which is structurally better suited to polygenic architecture than a 24-variant GWS-hits score. Despite being from a cross-disease comparison paper, the combination of genome-wide construction plus explicit OR evidence makes PGS002767 better-supported than PGS002729’s covariate-inflated full-model AUROC.

PGS000708 has closer endpoint fidelity to the target concept as a direct “Kidney failure” trait with a specified kidney-failure phenotype (though restricted to “Diabetic kidney failure”), and it provides more interpretable outcome evidence (time-to-event C-index 0.779 plus HR per SD 1.19 with CI) with clearly stated basic covariates (age/sex/PCs/batch), suggesting limited clinical leakage. PGS004492 maps to kidney failure via ICD code N18 “Chronic renal failure” (also aligned), but it has weaker visible support: covariates are unknown, no discrimination metrics are reported, and only a modest OR per SD (~1.17) without uncertainty. With both lacking PRS-only AUC/R2 and both EUR-only UKB-based, the better-documented endpoint/analysis package and slightly stronger evidence package favors PGS000708, but confidence is low because PGS000708’s phenotype is a diabetic subtype while PGS004492 is a broader chronic renal failure code.

PGS005218 is better-supported for hypothyroidism because it comes from a disease-focused hypothyroidism GWAS/prediction study with much broader multi-cohort development (23andMe, FinnGen, UKB, deCODE, etc.), far larger evaluation (n=441,692 vs 8,417), and a genome-wide shrinkage approach (PRS-CS; 1,110,091 variants) that is structurally more appropriate for a polygenic disease than the very sparse SnpNet score in PGS004935 (6,127 variants) from a portability-style UKB-only paper. Neither record provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported full-model AUROCs are not directly comparable PRS metrics; moreover PGS005218’s very high AUROC (0.859) is explicitly biomarker-augmented (TSH, T4, anti-TPO), making it largely non-informative about PRS-alone performance, while PGS004935’s AUROC=0.7 has unknown covariates and limited validation context. PGS004935 does report a strong OR per SD (~1.5), but given its framework/portability archetype and sparse construction, the overall evidence package still favors the disease-focused, genome-wide PGS005218.

PGS002729 is the better-supported knee osteoarthritis PRS because it is clearly disease-focused with direct endpoint framing (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: clinical osteoarthritis; trait_efo: osteoarthritis, knee), uses transparent basic covariates (age, sex, BMI), and provides an interpretable discrimination result (full-model AUROC 0.66 with CI) in a defined European validation sample (n=14,926) with multi-cohort development context. In contrast, PGS004549 comes from a risk-factor integration/metaPRS framework (RFDiseasemetaPRS) with unknown covariates (raising comparability/packaging concerns), provides no AUC/R2 or other discrimination metric (only a moderate OR=1.37), and is developed in a single cohort (UKB), making its standalone PRS evidence and external-transfer support weaker despite its very large variant count and larger validation n.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all hypertrophic cardiomyopathy), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not a reliable cross-model discriminator. PGS000739’s higher full-model AUROC (0.821 vs 0.73) is heavily discounted because it is explicitly adjusted for substantial clinical predictors and rare-variant carrier status (obesity, HTN, AF, CAD, HCM-ACMG carrier status, etc.), making the metric more covariate-driven and less comparable to standalone PRS performance. In contrast, PGS004910 uses only basic demographic/PC covariates (age, age^2, sex, PC1-10), provides supportive PRS effect-size evidence (HR 1.97; OR 1.26 per SD; OR 5.5 high vs median tertile), and is a genome-wide shrinkage PRS-CS model with far broader variant coverage (374,190 vs 27), which is a positive structural signal for a polygenic disease. Despite PGS004910 also only showing full-model metrics, its cleaner covariate design and stronger PRS-specific effect-size reporting make it better-supported for external PRS benchmarking than the clinically packaged PGS000739.

PGS000328 is better aligned to the generic target of lupus erythematosus as a disease-risk PRS: it targets systemic lupus erythematosus with a clearer disease-focused framing, whereas PGS000196’s phenotyping is explicitly restricted to “SLE diagnosis in patient with arthritis,” which is a more context-conditioned outpatient differential-diagnosis setting and less faithful to general SLE risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so the small AUROC difference (0.83 vs 0.79) is weak evidence; however, PGS000328 also has a larger validation sample (n=1,001 vs n=245) and slightly more variants (57 vs 55), providing modest additional support once endpoint fidelity is considered.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; trait_efo lung carcinoma; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer) and are EUR-trained/EUR-evaluated, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R², so full-model AUROC is not directly comparable as a standalone PRS metric. However, PGS004860 has stronger structural support for capturing polygenic signal (LDpred2 with ~1.14M variants vs PGS000078 genome-wide significant hits with 109 variants) and a moderately stronger per-SD effect size (OR=1.33 vs HR=1.16), suggesting higher PRS discriminative power. PGS000078’s very large validation sample is supportive but its reported performance is heavily bundled with extensive non-genetic risk factors (family history, detailed smoking variables and interactions, PM2.5), making the full-model AUROC less informative about PRS strength; PGS004860 uses a comparatively simpler covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking/PCs), reducing packaging/leakage concerns.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_reported lung cancer; phenotyping_reported incident lung cancer; EUR GWAS/EVAL). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the very high full-model AUROCs are not directly comparable as PRS metrics, especially given covariate differences. PGS000789 is heavily packaged with non-genetic risk factors (family history, detailed smoking intensity/duration plus interaction terms, PM2.5), making its full-model AUROC/C-index largely covariate-driven and less informative about standalone PRS quality. PGS004860 uses a genome-wide LDpred2 score (1,143,554 variants) with a lighter, more standard covariate set (age/sex/BMI/smoking status/PCs), and shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.33 vs HR 1.17), which is more indicative of PRS discriminative signal when PRS-only metrics are absent. Despite smaller validation n, the structural method/variant-count advantage and cleaner packaging make PGS004860 better-supported for likely external PRS performance.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are identical: incident lung cancer; EUR-only GWAS/EVAL; same covariates including smoking variables and family history; same validation n=392,539) and report essentially identical full-model discrimination (AUROC 0.846; C-index 0.849) with very similar HR per SD (1.16 vs 1.17). Candidate_b (PGS000789) is explicitly derived from candidate_a with inverse weights, which is a structural red flag for being a non-standard/less biologically coherent construction rather than an independently optimized PRS; its additional reported R²=0.799 is a full-model/ambiguous metric and is implausibly high relative to the lung cancer heritability ceiling, so it should not be used as evidence of stronger PRS signal. With no clean PRS-only AUC/R² for either, the original GWAS-hits score (PGS000078) is better-supported than an inverted-weight derivative (PGS000789).

Both candidates map cleanly to systemic lupus erythematosus (same trait_reported/trait_efo) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. Candidate_a (PGS000328) has a notable endpoint restriction (phenotyping_reported: onset before age 20), which is a narrower pediatric/early-onset subtype and less faithful to the generic target trait “lupus erythematosus” than candidate_b’s general SLE phenotyping. Candidate_b (PGS000754) also has stronger structural properties for a polygenic disease (lassosum with ~293k variants vs 57 GWAS-significant hits), and it is evaluated on a much larger sample (n=7,733 vs n=1,001) with a mixed-ancestry evaluation including EUR. Although PGS000328 shows a higher full-model AUROC (0.83 vs 0.65), without PRS-only/incremental metrics and with the early-onset endpoint restriction, that advantage is less reliable for benchmarking generic SLE risk than PGS000754’s broader endpoint and genome-wide construction.

Both candidates are near-clones: same publication, same target trait/EFO, same endpoint (incident invasive melanoma), same covariates (age, sex), same EUR-only GWAS/EVAL ancestry, and same validation sample size (n=4,765). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (only full-model AUROC/R²), so performance evidence is only weakly differentiating. In this same-context tie-break, PGS002247 has a modestly higher full-model AUROC (0.691 vs 0.688) and R² (0.072 vs 0.070) and also includes more genome-wide significant variants (68 vs 50), which is a moderate positive structural signal within the same method family. The differences are small, so confidence is moderate.

Both candidates map cleanly to the target concept via trait_efo (osteoarthritis, knee) and neither reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so we fall back to endpoint fidelity, covariate transparency, and effect-size support. PGS002767 is a direct knee osteoarthritis endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both ‘Knee osteoarthritis’) with clearly stated basic covariates (age, sex, PCs, technical), reducing concern about risk-factor/clinical packaging. PGS004549 uses an ICD-style label (M17 gonarthrosis) and comes from a ‘risk factor PRS + disease PRS integration’ archetype with unknown covariates, which raises comparability/packaging uncertainty even though its OR is similar and it has a larger training/validation N. With near-tied ORs (~1.35 vs ~1.37) and similar EUR-only context, the cleaner endpoint/covariate evidence slightly favors PGS002767.

Both candidates match the target well (trait_efo lymphoid leukemia; phenotyping_reported Incident Lymphocytic Leukemia) and use the same basic covariates, with no PRS-only AUC/R² reported in either record (so full-model AUROC/C-index are not clean PRS comparators). PGS000788 is explicitly constructed as “75 variants from Graff et al (PGS000077) with inverse variant weights,” i.e., a sign-flipped version of the same SNP set, which is a strong negative support signal versus the original. While PGS000788 shows slightly higher full-model AUROC/C-index and HR, those are within the same covariate-adjusted framework and don’t outweigh that it is an inversely weighted derivative rather than a directly supported PRS. Therefore the better-supported, more plausible-to-transfer model is the original PGS000077.

Both candidates align to the target (trait_efo=lymphoid leukemia), but PGS000077 has stronger overall support: it uses a substantially richer GWAS-hits score (75 variants vs 6 for PGS000645) and shows a stronger PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.45 vs OR per SD 1.358), suggesting better standalone genetic discrimination. Its evaluation is also far broader (EUR n=391,338 vs n=957), increasing reliability of the reported association. Although both only report full-model AUROC (not PRS-only), PGS000077’s covariates are still basic (age/sex/PCs/array) and its higher full-model AUROC (0.719 vs 0.578) is at least directionally consistent with the stronger effect size, whereas PGS000645’s very sparse P+T construction and small development/validation context make it less likely to rank highly in external benchmarks.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (late-onset Alzheimer’s disease in trait_efo; phenotyping_reported is late-onset AD for both, with PGS000053 specifying familial late-onset LOAD but still aligned). Neither provides clean PRS-only AUC/R², so performance must be judged via other visible evidence. PGS000053 has a directly PRS-informative effect size (OR per SD 1.29, moderate signal) and uses only basic covariates (age, sex), reducing concerns about covariate-driven inflation. PGS000334 reports only a variance-explained R²=0.191 that appears to be a full-model/unspecified metric (not PRS-only) with covariates listed as unknown; given the simple C+T method and the trait heritability ceiling context, this high R² is less trustworthy/comparable. With more coherent PRS-specific evidence and cleaner covariate disclosure, PGS000053 is better-supported than PGS000334.

PGS004606 is better supported for the generic target “macular degeneration” because its endpoint is directly aligned (phenotyping_reported: Age-related macular degeneration) and it shows stronger PRS signal via effect size (OR per SD 1.76 vs 1.41 for PGS004952). Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the much higher full-model AUROC reported for PGS004952 (0.842) is not a reliable standalone PRS discriminator—especially given similar basic covariates—while PGS004606 also has a far larger validation sample (163,011 vs 1,232), increasing trust in the stability of its reported association. PGS004952 additionally targets a narrower endpoint (“Late” AMD clinical classification), which is a mild mismatch versus the broader AMD target.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Multiple myeloma”; trait_efo both plasma cell myeloma), method (genome-wide significant variants), variant count (23), and ancestry (EUR GWAS/EVAL). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC difference (0.69 in PGS002306 vs 0.644 in PGS002281) is not a reliable PRS discriminator, especially with different/unknown covariates. PGS002281 has cleaner, explicitly stated basic covariates (age, sex, geographic region) and provides an additional effect-size signal (OR highest vs lowest quintile 3.18), whereas PGS002306 lists covariates as unknown and lacks supporting OR/HR metrics. Given the otherwise tied structure, the cleaner covariate transparency and extra effect-size evidence favor PGS002281, but confidence is low because the records are highly similar and both rely on full-model AUROC.

PGS002246 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target trait melanoma: its phenotyping is "Incident invasive melanoma" in prospective cohorts, which is closer to general melanoma risk prediction than PGS000813’s restricted high-risk subgroup phenotype ("Familial cutaneous melanoma in non-carriers of a CDKN2A mutation"), which may not transfer to population-based benchmarks. Both candidates lack PRS-only AUC/R2 and use similarly light covariates (age, sex), so PGS000813’s higher reported AUROC (0.77 vs 0.688) is only a full-model metric and is not reliably comparable across these different ascertainment settings; its strong ORs likely reflect familial enrichment. With ancestry context similar (EUR-only evaluation) and variant counts similar (50 vs 46), the more general, incident-disease endpoint in PGS002246 is the stronger-supported choice for external benchmark performance.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (age-related macular degeneration) with identical phenotyping and basic covariates (age, sex, PCs 1–10) and are from the same Nat Genet study with the same EUR evaluation sample size (n=163,011), so this is a near-clone comparison where within-context performance/effect size can break the tie. PGS004606 shows stronger apparent predictive signal in the selected validation record (full-model AUROC 0.71 vs 0.65 for PGS004607) and a materially higher per-SD effect size (OR 1.76 [1.73–1.78] vs 1.48 [1.34–1.63]). Additionally, PGS004606 is trained on EUR GWAS (IAMDGC) matching the EUR evaluation ancestry, whereas PGS004607 is trained on AFR GWAS (MVP) but evaluated in EUR, a transportability mismatch that plausibly contributes to its weaker observed performance. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the stronger OR and higher AUROC under comparable covariates favor PGS004606.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Multiple myeloma”, EFO plasma cell myeloma) and similar sparse GWAS-hit construction (23 vs 22 variants) in EUR-only evaluation, with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either (so full-model AUROC is only weakly comparable). Given similarly basic covariates (PGS002281: age/sex/region; PGS000653: age/sex/PCs/batch), the materially higher reported discrimination and stratification in the selected validation for PGS002281 (full-model AUROC 0.644; OR highest vs lowest quintiles 3.18) versus PGS000653 (AUROC 0.577; OR top 1% vs rest 2.2 with wide CI crossing 1) provides the stronger visible support. PGS000653’s framework/repository context (Cancer PRSweb) and modest per-SD OR (1.33) do not outweigh PGS002281’s stronger observed performance in a similar EUR setting.

PGS000754 is better supported for the target trait because its endpoint fidelity is clean (phenotyping_reported is simply “Systemic lupus erythematosus”), whereas PGS000196’s endpoint is explicitly restricted/packaged (“Systemic lupus erythematosus diagnosis in patient with arthritis”), which is a narrower clinical-ascertainment context and less directly aligned to generic lupus erythematosus risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (both only show full-model AUROC), so PGS000196’s higher AUROC (0.79 vs 0.65) is not a reliable PRS-comparable advantage, especially with covariates unknown in both. With metrics unable to cleanly differentiate, structural signals favor PGS000754: a genome-wide shrinkage-style method (lassosum) with far more variants (293,684 vs 55) and a larger validation sample (7,733 vs 245), plus some multi-ancestry evaluation, making it more likely to transfer well in external benchmarking than the sparse P+T 55-variant outpatient-arthritis-context score.

Both candidates match the target well (AMD; EFO aligned) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROCs (0.842 in PGS004952 vs 0.65 in PGS004607) are not directly comparable PRS metrics. With metrics largely non-comparable, structural and effect-size evidence matter more: PGS004607 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with ~1.07M variants and shows a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.48 vs 1.41 for PGS004952), consistent with capturing more polygenic signal. PGS004952 is a 52-SNP genome-wide-significant score and its very high AUROC is likely dominated by covariates/endpoint specifics (late AMD clinical classification) rather than demonstrating superior standalone PRS performance. Despite the GWAS ancestry mismatch (AFR training, EUR eval) lowering confidence, PGS004607’s method/coverage and stronger OR make it the better-supported bet for external benchmark ranking.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match) and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2, so the reported AUROCs are full-model and not directly comparable as PRS performance. Given that, PGS000809 is better-supported because it reports a transparent, basic covariate set (age, sex, PCs 1–2), making its full-model AUROC/R2 less likely to be driven by undisclosed clinical augmentation, whereas PGS002726 has covariates listed as Unknown, reducing interpretability of its slightly higher full-model AUROC (0.80 vs 0.765). Although PGS002726 uses far more variants and reports a strong top-decile OR, the unclear method label (“Genome-wide significant variants” despite 476,399 variants) plus unknown covariates makes its performance evidence less reliable on the visible fields than PGS000809’s cleaner evaluation context and multi-cohort development listing.

PGS002247 has better endpoint fidelity to the generic target trait melanoma: it evaluates an incident invasive melanoma endpoint in prospective cohorts, which is closer to general melanoma risk prediction than PGS000813’s restricted familial cutaneous melanoma in CDKN2A non-carriers (a special high-risk subgroup that may not transfer to a general benchmark setting). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R², so the higher full-model AUROC in PGS000813 (0.77 vs 0.691) is not a reliable PRS discriminator; both use only age/sex covariates, making full-model AUC differences less interpretable across different study populations. Given the broader, more generalizable phenotype framing and external-cohort evaluation context, PGS002247 is better-supported for melanoma overall despite lacking strong PRS-isolated metrics.

The two candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and method (LDpred), same variant count, same MVP development cohort, same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same multi-ancestry evaluation setup and identical validation sample size. Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model C-index is only a weak within-family tie-break. On the selected European validation record, PGS005039 is marginally stronger than PGS005035 on both reported full-model C-index (0.7848 vs 0.7834) and per-SD OR (1.578 vs 1.541), so PGS005039 is the better-supported pick, though the differences are small.

PGS000788 is better-supported for the target lymphoid leukemia because it shows materially stronger genetic signal and broader development/validation context while maintaining acceptable endpoint alignment. Both candidates map to the same EFO trait and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R² (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator), but PGS000788 reports a strong per-SD effect size (HR=1.7) versus PGS000645’s more modest per-SD OR=1.358, which is a more informative indicator of PRS discrimination in the absence of PRS-only metrics. Structurally, PGS000788 uses many more variants (75 vs 6) and is derived from an established leukemia PRS (Graff et al) and evaluated in a very large European sample (n=391,338) with only basic covariates; PGS000645 is a sparse P+T score trained/developed in a single cohort (MGI; training n=1,100) with a much smaller evaluation (n=957). Although PGS000645’s trait label is slightly closer and it reports an OR top 1% vs rest, its overall evidence package (very low variant count, small eval, weaker per-SD effect) is less likely to rank higher in external benchmarking than PGS000788.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication/study family, same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), identical ancestry distributions and validation sample size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). With endpoint and design effectively identical, the only differentiators are small within-family performance/effect-size differences: PGS005045 has a marginally higher full-model C-index (0.78385 vs 0.78336) and slightly higher OR per SD (1.554 vs 1.541). These differences are tiny, so confidence is low, but they favor PGS005045.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment to multiple sclerosis (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match). PGS002038 comes from a UKB portability framework paper and reports only a weak PRS-comparable signal (partial-r=0.0396) despite large validation n=19,299; such framework-derived scores are explicitly noted to underperform disease-focused alternatives when available. PGS002726 is disease-focused (IMSGC; MS susceptibility/phenotype in Europeans) and shows much stronger discrimination evidence on-record via a very large risk stratification effect (OR top 10% vs median = 15.0) plus an AUROC=0.8 (though this appears to be full-model and covariates are unknown, so it’s discounted). Given the framework penalty and the stronger disease-specific effect-size evidence, PGS002726 is better-supported for likely external performance.

Both candidates are near-clones: same MI PheCode 411.2 endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all aligned), same publication and release date, same training cohort (MVP), same covariates (age, sex, 20 PCs), same ancestry distribution and validation sample size (n=30,379), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model C-index). In this tie-like setting, the only differentiators are the within-study performance/effect-size signals: PGS005039 has a slightly higher full-model C-index (0.78484 vs 0.78385) and a slightly stronger per-SD OR (1.578 vs 1.554) than PGS005045, so it is marginally better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones: same reported trait/EFO (benign nodular goiter), same phenotyping string (typoed but matching), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%) and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC shown, which is not a strong cross-model discriminator). In this same-study, same-endpoint context, the small but consistent performance/effect-size edge favors PGS005262: higher full-model AUROC (0.5933 vs 0.5876) and stronger effect sizes (OR 1.408 vs 1.362; β 0.342 vs 0.309). PGS005263’s slightly smaller variant count and fewer listed development cohorts do not offset that.

Both candidates target the same endpoint (benign nodular goiter) with identical phenotyping string, ancestry distribution, cohorts, and validation sample size, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model AUROC, which is not a reliable PRS comparator). In this near-clone setting, structural and effect-size evidence are the best differentiators: PGS005262 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a much stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.41, β≈0.34) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T score with 110 variants and weak effect (OR≈1.05, β≈0.05). The small full-model AUROC difference (0.593 vs 0.585) is minor, but it is directionally consistent with PGS005262 being stronger.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), ancestry (EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL), training cohort (UKB) and validation size (n=5,196), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (only full-model metrics, which are weak differentiators). In this same-study, same-endpoint setting, PGS000550 has consistently slightly stronger empirical signals than PGS000549: higher full-model AUROC (0.568 vs 0.567), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0113 vs 0.00996), and higher per-SD OR (1.286 vs 1.263). Structurally it is also a genome-wide PRS-CS score with far more variants (1,115,189 vs 16 GWAS hits), which is generally favored for polygenic signal capture when other fields are matched. The differences are small, so confidence is moderate rather than high.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical endpoint framing (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported: Tobacco use disorder; trait_efo: nicotine dependence), identical training cohort and size (UKB, n=391,124), identical basic covariates, and the same validation sample size (n=19,400), with no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported for either—so performance must be separated by the comparable metric available and structural signals. PGS002037 shows higher PRS-comparable performance (partial-r 0.0741 vs 0.0557 for PGS001830) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far broader variant coverage (847,691 vs 13,838), which is generally favorable for polygenic traits when other fields are matched. With no countervailing evidence favoring PGS001830, PGS002037 is better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo and same phenotyping_reported typo), publication family, evaluation ancestry (MAE 100%), and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—only full-model AUROC, which is not a strong differentiator here. Given that, structural and effect-size evidence matter most: PGS005263 uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a materially stronger per-SD effect (OR≈1.36, β≈0.309) than PGS005261’s sparse P+T 110-variant score with weak effect (OR≈1.05, β≈0.047). The tiny full-model AUROC difference (0.588 vs 0.585) is essentially noise, so the stronger method/coverage and effect-size support favor PGS005263.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (ICD10 J33 nasal polyp; EFO Nasal Cavity Polyp), publication/study family (same Commun Biol paper), ancestry (EUR dev/eval), training cohort (UKB), variant count (1,059,939), and they lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and have unknown covariates—so performance must be inferred from the remaining comparable evidence. The main differentiator is effect size: PGS004535 reports a materially stronger OR per SD (1.60) than PGS004465 (1.35), which domain guidance treats as a strong predictor of real-world PRS discrimination when AUC/R2 are absent. Although PGS004465 uses LDpred2 (a strong single-score shrinkage method), PGS004535’s meta/ensemble-style method label (RFDiseasemetaPRS) plus the stronger OR provides the better-supported expectation of higher benchmark performance in this same-endpoint sibling comparison.

PGS003385 is less perfectly aligned to the broad target (it is ovarian serous carcinoma rather than ovarian neoplasm overall), but it is still a closely related ovarian cancer endpoint and is supported by a much stronger PRS construction (lassosum, 144,810 variants) than PGS000549’s very sparse GWAS-hits score (16 variants). Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the higher reported AUROC for PGS003385 (0.717 vs 0.567) is only full-model and not decisive, but with similarly basic covariates (age+PCs; PGS000549 also includes batch and sex) the large structural advantage and substantially better reported discrimination favor PGS003385 over the older, low-variant framework-style repository score PGS000549.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity and study context: same reported trait/phenotyping (“Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation”), same EFO mapping, same UKB portability publication, identical training cohort (UKB), training N (391,124), covariates (sex, age, birth date, deprivation index, 16 PCs), ancestry distribution, and validation size (20,000). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the only comparable performance signal is partial correlation, where PGS002033 is higher (partial-r 0.0789 vs 0.0547 for PGS001825). Structurally, PGS002033 also uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with far more variants (846,292 vs 13,009), which is a positive signal for a highly polygenic trait like obesity when other fields are matched. Therefore PGS002033 is better-supported than PGS001825.

PGS005235 has higher endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity: its phenotyping_reported is an explicit obesity diagnosis code ("Obesity (phecode: 278.1)") and trait_efo is obesity, whereas PGS002033 is a broader administrative bundle ("Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation" / overnutrition) from a UKB portability framework. Neither candidate reports PRS-comparable AUC/R2, but PGS005235 provides supportive PRS discrimination evidence via a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.97), while PGS002033 only reports a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.079). Although PGS002033 has multi-ancestry evaluation, its framework/portability archetype and weaker phenotype specificity make it less likely to rank highest for obesity than the diagnosis-anchored, effect-size-supported PGS005235.

PGS002768 is the better-supported choice for generic osteoporosis risk: its phenotyping_reported is a direct osteoporosis endpoint (vs PGS001274’s time-to-event “osteoporosis without pathological fracture,” a narrower/horizon-style framing), and it comes from a cross-disease but disease-endpoint-focused comparison paper rather than the known pan-trait UKB sparse-framework archetype (“across 813 traits”) that is penalized for weaker external transfer. Although PGS001274 reports clean PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.576, R2 0.00945) and multi-ancestry evaluation, those metrics are modest and the model is very sparse (1,270 variants, snpnet) consistent with the framework pattern; by contrast PGS002768 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRS-CS) with ~1.09M variants and shows a moderate per-SD OR=1.31, supporting meaningful PRS signal despite missing PRS-only AUC/R2. Overall, endpoint fidelity plus stronger structural method/coverage outweigh PGS001274’s modest PRS-only metrics from a framework score.

PGS005235 has stronger endpoint fidelity to the target trait obesity via an explicit diagnosis-based phenotype ("Obesity (phecode: 278.1)") and is developed from multi-cohort obesity/adiposity GWAS sources (EGG/GIANT/UKB) using a genome-wide shrinkage method (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (709,828). It also provides supportive PRS discrimination evidence via a strong per-SD effect size (OR≈1.97). In contrast, PGS001825 comes from a UKB portability framework paper ("Portability of 245 polygenic scores"), uses a more generic/bundled phenotype label ("Overweight, obesity and other hyperalimentation"), and its only visible performance signal is a modest partial correlation (partial-r≈0.055) without PRS-comparable R2/AUC or effect sizes. Although PGS001825 has multi-ancestry evaluation, the combination of weaker phenotype specificity and weaker PRS-signal evidence makes it less likely to rank higher than PGS005235.

Both candidates target the same disease concept (Pancreatic cancer; EFO exocrine pancreatic carcinoma) and use the same GWAS-hits construction (22 variants) with the same listed development cohorts, and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is not a clean PRS comparator). Given that, PGS000083 is better-supported on the visible evidence: it has a stronger PRS-associated effect size (HR per SD 1.49 vs PGS000663 OR 1.44) and its evaluation is a large, general incident pancreatic cancer setting (n=391,491) without horizon-conditioned packaging. In contrast, PGS000663’s endpoint is explicitly horizon-specific (“0–10 years of follow-up”) and its covariates include diabetic status (a stronger mediator/clinical predictor), making its full-model AUROC (0.67) less informative for standalone PRS ranking. Overall, PGS000083 looks more endpoint-faithful and less clinically packaged, with slightly stronger genetic signal.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported), covariates (basic demographics + PCs), training cohort/size (UKB; n=391,124), and evaluation ancestry mix/validation N (n=19,668), all from the same portability paper—so the tie-break is within-family performance and structural signals. PGS002055 (LDpred2, genome-wide shrinkage; 599,514 variants) shows a higher selected European partial correlation (partial-r=0.0175 vs 0.0151 for PGS001843) with overlapping but slightly better CI, and it uses a genome-wide model rather than an extremely sparse 242-variant penalized regression score. With no PRS-only AUC/R2 available for either, the modestly better partial-r plus stronger polygenic capture favors PGS002055.

Both candidates target otosclerosis, but PGS002046 has cleaner endpoint fidelity (phenotyping_reported simply “Otosclerosis” vs PGS001255’s time-to-event “TTE otosclerosis”, which is a mild mismatch for a generic disease target) and a stronger structural model (LDpred2 genome-wide shrinkage with 570,308 variants vs a very sparse snpnet model with 213 variants from the pan-trait “813 traits” framework, which is a known weaker archetype for external transfer). PGS001255 does provide explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.6319; PGS-only R2 0.01341) that are plausible under the heritability ceiling, but given its framework/sparse construction and TTE framing, that metric advantage is not enough to outweigh PGS002046’s more robust genome-wide construction and more direct phenotype framing. Confidence is low because PGS002046 lacks PRS-comparable AUROC/R2, leaving only partial-r (0.0182) as performance evidence.

PGS005217 is a disease-focused PAD score with high endpoint fidelity to the target (peripheral vascular disease) via a near-synonymous clinical diagnosis endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”), developed/validated in a large multi-cohort, multi-ancestry setting (many cohorts; EVAL n=304,294 across multiple ancestries). It also provides supportive PRS signal via an HR per SD of 1.66, consistent with meaningful discrimination, and uses only basic covariates (age/sex/PCs) without obvious clinical-risk packaging. In contrast, PGS001843 is from a UKB portability framework paper with a vague/unspecified phenotype (“Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”) and shows very weak PRS evidence (partial-r=0.0151), despite a larger UKB training sample; its framework archetype and sparse 242-variant construction are less likely to transfer well than the disease-specific, genome-wide LDpred2 model.

Both candidates have strong endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to multiple myeloma/plasma cell myeloma) and both are sparse GWAS-hit style scores with similar variant counts (PGS002306: 23 vs PGS000653: 22) in EUR-only evaluation. However, PGS000653 is better-supported on visible PRS-relevant evidence: it reports PRS effect sizes (OR per SD 1.327, plus top-1% vs rest OR) and includes explicit basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), making its evaluation context clearer and less ambiguous than PGS002306’s unknown covariates. PGS002306’s only reported metric is a full-model AUROC (0.69) without PRS-only metrics or effect sizes, which is not comparable as standalone PRS performance and could be covariate-driven. Given the lack of PRS-only AUC/R2 for both, the presence of interpretable PRS effect-size evidence and clearer evaluation specification favors PGS000653 despite its lower full-model AUROC.

PGS003586 is the better-supported match for the target trait preeclampsia: its trait_reported is explicitly “Pre-eclampsia” (direct endpoint fidelity), whereas PGS003587 is reported as “Gestational hypertension” despite sharing the same phenotyping_reported string. Both are near-clones otherwise (same Nat Med paper, PRS-CS, ~1.09M variants, EUR-only development/evaluation, identical validation N and covariates, and no PRS-only AUC/R2). With metrics absent, the tie-break comes from endpoint alignment and available effect size: PGS003586 also shows a stronger per-SD OR (1.31 vs 1.20), supporting better discriminative signal in the same study context.

PGS000902 is better-supported as a standalone Parkinson’s disease PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis with explicit multi-cohort development (23andMe/IPDGC/UKB etc.) and uses a larger GWAS-hit set (90 variants vs 44). While neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, PGS000902 at least provides a (covariate-adjusted) AUROC=0.651 with basic covariates (age/sex/PCs), whereas PGS003763 provides only a tertile HR (1.72) from an incident PD frailty-focused study context and lacks any training/development details (samples_training N/A), making its PRS evidence less directly anchored to a dedicated PD genetics model despite its large evaluation N.

PGS003587 is better-supported for the target trait preeclampsia because its endpoint evidence is more coherent: although trait_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” both trait_efo and phenotyping_reported explicitly anchor to pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, matching the target disease concept. It also comes from a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort development (multiple listed biobanks; training n=212,034) with basic covariates (maternal age, age^2, PCs) and provides an OR per SD of 1.20 as PRS signal. In contrast, PGS004593 has internal inconsistencies (trait_reported “Preeclampsia” but phenotyping_reported “Gestational hypertension”), lacks any training/development cohort detail and training sample size, and its HR=1.16 suggests slightly weaker PRS signal; its much larger validation N is only a weak tie-break per the provided guidance.

Both candidates are near-clone snpnet scores from the same UKB pan-trait framework paper with identical training size (n=269,704), covariates (age, sex, array, PCs), and validation context (EUR-selected; n=24,905; same ancestry distribution). Candidate_b (PGS001274) has slightly better PRS-only metrics (AUROC 0.57595 vs 0.5685; R2 0.00945 vs 0.00688) and more variants (1270 vs 316), but it targets a narrower time-to-event endpoint ('osteoporosis without pathological fracture'), which is a phenotype-fidelity mismatch for the generic target trait 'osteoporosis'. Candidate_a (PGS001273) matches the generic osteoporosis endpoint directly in trait_reported/phenotyping_reported, so despite slightly weaker PRS-only performance, it is better aligned to the benchmark target; the small metric gap is not decisive given the endpoint mismatch.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (phenotyping_reported and trait_reported are Osteoporosis), but PGS001273 is a classic pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-framework score (“across 813 traits”, snpnet, 316 variants), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer than disease-focused scores unless it has clearly superior endpoint+metric evidence. Its PRS-only metrics are modest (PGS-only AUROC 0.5685; PGS-only R2 0.00688) and the high full-model AUROC (0.7897) is largely covariate-driven given the tiny incremental AUROC (0.00477). PGS002768, while lacking PRS-only AUC/R2, comes from a disease-comparative but not pan-trait framework setting and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS) with very large variant coverage (~1.09M) and shows a moderate per-SD effect size (OR 1.31, 95% CI 1.25–1.38) in a larger EUR evaluation (n=39,444 vs 24,905). Given the framework penalty and weak PRS-only performance for PGS001273, PGS002768 is better-supported as the more likely higher-performing osteoporosis PRS.

PGS005217 is better supported for the target concept despite not having PRS-only AUC/R2: it is a disease-focused PAD model with a clear clinical endpoint (“Incident peripheral artery disease”) and provides a strong PRS effect size (HR per SD 1.66, 95% CI 1.61–1.71) plus broad multi-ancestry evaluation and large validation (n=304,294). Its reported C-index 0.731 is full-model (age/sex/PCs) and thus not directly comparable as PRS-only, but the strong HR still supports meaningful PRS signal. In contrast, PGS002055 comes from a UKB portability framework (“Portability of 245 polygenic scores…”) with a vaguer endpoint (“Peripheral vascular disease, unspecified”) and only a very small PRS-comparable metric (partial-r 0.0175), with much smaller validation (n=19,668). Given endpoint fidelity and stronger discriminative evidence via effect size, PGS005217 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same Lancet Neurol PD GWAS meta-analysis with identical phenotype/covariates (Parkinson’s disease; PCs 1–5, age, sex), same training cohorts and training N, and same validation sample size (n=999), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R². In this same-endpoint sibling comparison, PGS000903 has materially stronger supportive performance/effect evidence: higher reported AUROC (0.692 vs 0.651 for PGS000902) and it additionally reports R²=0.054 plus a strong stratification OR (top vs bottom quartile OR=6.25), whereas PGS000902 lacks these supporting metrics/effect sizes. PGS000903 also uses a denser C+T score (1805 variants) versus a sparse genome-wide-significant-hits score (90 variants), which is a positive structural signal when other fields are matched.

Both candidates are near-clones: same prostate cancer endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication family, same training cohort (UKB) and training N (9,671), same ancestry distribution and validation size (n=171,474), and both report only full-model (not PGS-only) AUROC/R² with covariates listed as 0. In this same-context comparison, PGS004155 has consistently stronger reported performance/effect-size signals than PGS004042 (higher full-model AUROC 0.7049 vs 0.6994; higher R² 0.1280 vs 0.1202; higher OR per SD 2.166 vs 2.112), and it also uses an ensemble/multi-score method (UKBB-EUR.MultiPRS.CV) which is a positive structural signal over a single-score LDpred2.CV when other fields are matched. Given the framework penalty on sparse models and the structural advantage of genome-wide shrinkage for polygenic traits, PGS002083 is better-supported to rank higher externally despite weaker direct metric reporting.

Both candidates align to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, but PGS001791 has stronger PRS-supporting evidence on the visible fields: it reports a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only/covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.005929) that is plausible under the pulmonary fibrosis h2_obs ceiling (0.0039) and at least provides directly comparable PRS signal, whereas PGS004695 provides no PRS-only AUC/R2 and only an HR (high vs low quintile=3.78) without per-SD scaling, making cross-model PRS strength harder to benchmark. PGS004695’s incident IPF framing and environmental/epidemiologic covariate set are not disqualifying, but the sparse SNP set plus lack of PRS-comparable performance metrics leaves it less well-supported than PGS001791 for expected benchmark ranking.

Both candidates are UKB-derived framework/portability-style scores with broadly aligned endpoints to retinal detachment, but PGS001137 has cleaner, directly PRS-comparable performance reported (PGS-only AUROC=0.573 and PGS-only R2=0.00663) under basic covariates, and its PRS-only R2 is plausible relative to the provided h2_obs ceiling (~0.0042) as a sanity check (same order of magnitude, not wildly inflated). Although PGS005220 reports only a full-model AUROC (0.79) and includes BMI as a covariate (so the AUROC is not PRS-comparable), it still shows a substantially stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.53) than PGS003213, and the framework penalty plus weak effect size for PGS003213 makes it less likely to rank highly in external benchmarks.

Both candidates are near-clones: same thyroid carcinoma endpoint (trait_efo and phenotyping_reported match), same method (PRSCS), same evaluation ancestry mix and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and both lack PRS-only AUC/R2 with covariates unknown—so full-model AUROC is only a weak tie-break. Within this same-publication sibling context, PGS005259 has consistently stronger visible performance signals than PGS005260: higher full-model AUROC (0.695 vs 0.685) and higher effect sizes (OR 2.04 vs 1.96; β 0.711 vs 0.673), with essentially identical variant counts. The slightly broader listed training cohort set in PGS005259 is minor support but not decisive; the main differentiator is the stronger AUROC/effect-size package.

Both candidates have good endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all align to type 1 diabetes). PGS001297 provides clean PRS-only metrics (PGS AUROC 0.771, PGS R2 0.091) with only basic covariates, but it comes from a pan-trait UK Biobank sparse-score framework (“across 813 traits”, snpnet), which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer than disease-focused models. PGS000024 is explicitly disease-focused (T1D genetic risk score for screening/diagnosis; developed in T1DGC) and shows broader multi-ancestry evaluation coverage in its ancestry_distribution, which is supportive for robustness even though it lacks PRS-only AUC/R2 and its reported AUROC=0.921 is full-model and not directly comparable. Given the framework penalty on PGS001297 and the disease-focused, multi-cohort nature plus broader evaluation context of PGS000024, PGS000024 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks despite weaker directly comparable metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones: same SCC endpoint (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all match), same publication/family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same training cohort (MGI) and size (n=8,029), same covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs1-4), and same validation size (n=8,473). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so we cannot use clean PRS-comparable metrics; we must rely on within-family full-model/effect-size differences. PGS000461 shows slightly better overall discrimination and fit (full-model AUROC 0.599 vs 0.593; Nagelkerke R² 0.0304 vs 0.0268; slightly higher per-SD OR 1.491 vs 1.448 and β 0.40 vs 0.37). Although PGS000463 has a marginally higher top-1% OR (3.74 vs 3.51), the broader metrics favor PGS000461, making it the better-supported pick in this matched comparison.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (trait_efo thyroid carcinoma; phenotyping_reported matches), publication/study family (same medRxiv paper), ancestry distribution (same MAE eval), cohorts, covariates (both unknown), and validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so full-model AUROC is only a weak tie-break. In this same-context comparison, PGS005259 is better-supported: it shows materially stronger effect-size evidence (OR 2.04 per SD; β 0.71) versus PGS005258’s near-null effect sizes (OR 1.02; β 0.016), and it also has slightly higher reported AUROC (0.695 vs 0.686). Structurally, PGS005259 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with ~1.09M variants versus P+T with 84 variants, which is a positive signal when other fields are matched.

Both candidates match the target trait cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so the full-model AUROC values (0.921 for PGS000024 vs 0.817 for PGS000023) are not strong cross-model PRS evidence. With PRS-comparable metrics absent for both, structural signals dominate: PGS000024 uses a much richer score (85 variants with interaction modelling) versus PGS000023’s very sparse 7-variant GWAS-hits score, which is less likely to capture polygenic signal. PGS000024 also shows broader evaluation ancestry distribution and much larger stated validation sample size (374,000 vs 57,643), which is mildly supportive. Overall, PGS000024 is better-supported as a standalone T1D PRS, while PGS000023 appears more ancestry-specific and underpowered structurally due to the extremely low variant count.

Both candidates are near-clones on endpoint fidelity (same trait_efo and phenotyping_reported), publication family, evaluation ancestry mix (MAE) and identical validation sample size (n=94,651), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2—so full-model AUROC differences (0.6845 vs 0.6862) are essentially noise. The main differentiators are structural and effect-size evidence: PGS005260 uses genome-wide shrinkage (PRSCS) with 1,085,170 variants and shows a strong per-SD effect (OR≈1.96, β≈0.67), consistent with meaningful PRS signal, whereas PGS005258 is a very sparse P+T score (84 variants) with a near-null reported effect (OR≈1.02, β≈0.016), suggesting weak standalone PRS contribution despite similar full-model AUROC. Therefore PGS005260 is better-supported as the stronger PRS.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all Type 1 diabetes). However, PGS001297 is from a known pan-trait UK Biobank framework (“across 813 traits”) using a sparse snpnet model, which domain guidance flags as systematically less reliable for external transfer despite having clean PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.771, R2 0.0912; R2 is below the EUR h2_liability ceiling so not obviously inflated). PGS000023 comes from a disease-focused, multi-cohort T1D study explicitly addressing African-ancestry risk and shows broader multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/EUR/others) with a very large validation sample (n=57,643), which is supportive of robustness/transportability; its reported AUROC (0.817) is full-model and thus not directly comparable, but it is not paired with any explicit heavy clinical covariate packaging. Given the strong penalty against pan-trait framework scores when a disease-focused alternative exists, PGS000023 is more likely to rank higher in external benchmarks despite weaker PRS-only metric reporting.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo and phenotyping_reported are direct T2D). Neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model/incremental metrics are not cleanly comparable as standalone PRS evidence. PGS004152 has stronger PRS-relevant support via a clear per-SD effect size (OR=1.67 with tight CI), which domain guidance treats as a meaningful discriminator when PRS-only metrics are absent; PGS004839 provides no effect sizes and only an incremental R2 from a covariate-adjusted model (age/sex/PCs), which is less directly interpretable for PRS strength. PGS004152 also shows broader evaluation ancestry coverage (EUR+GME+SAS) and much larger validation (n=90,274 vs 7,879), supporting robustness, while PGS004839 is evaluated on a smaller sample with limited ancestry breadth.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all T2D) and neither provides PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on study archetype, transportability, and effect-size evidence. PGS002308 comes from a disease-focused trans-ancestry T2D PRS development/validation study with broad multi-ancestry evaluation (AFR/AMR/EAS/EUR/GME) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.96), which is supportive of real PRS discrimination even without PRS-only metrics. PGS004839 is from a more general integrative/pan-trait-style framework paper, is developed in EUR-only (AllofUs) with limited evaluation breadth (EUR/GME), and its only performance signal is an incremental R2=0.129 that is not clearly PRS-only and is less comparable across studies. Given the domain guidance that disease-focused multi-cohort scores typically outperform framework-derived scores absent clearly superior comparable metrics, PGS002308 is better-supported.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same UKB portability paper with identical endpoint fidelity (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both “Urinary calculus”, trait_efo urolithiasis), identical covariates (age/sex/PCs etc.), identical training cohort/size (UKB n=391,124), and identical evaluation ancestry mix and validation N (n=19,913). With no PRS-only AUC/R2 for either, the main differentiators are the comparable PRS metric available (partial-r) and structural properties. PGS002075 has higher partial correlation (0.0385 vs 0.0323 for PGS001864) and is a genome-wide shrinkage score with far more variants (731,196 vs 5,599), which is generally favorable for capturing polygenic signal when all else is equal. Therefore PGS002075 is better-supported on the visible evidence.

PGS000903 is better-supported as a standalone PD PRS: it comes from a large, disease-focused GWAS meta-analysis (Lancet Neurol; multi-cohort IPDGC/23andMe/UKB etc.), uses a substantially richer score (1805 variants C+T), and provides stronger PRS-discrimination evidence via a large risk gradient (OR top vs bottom quartile 6.25) plus reported model metrics (though only full-model AUROC/R²). It also shows broader evaluation ancestry (EUR/MAE/SAS), suggesting some transportability evidence beyond EUR. In contrast, PGS003763 is a sparse 44-SNP genome-wide-significant score with no training details, only EUR evaluation, and reports only an HR (1.72 high vs low tertile) from an incident-PD time-to-event framing in a frailty-focused study, which is less directly informative for general PD PRS performance. Neither reports clean PGS-only AUC/R², so the stronger disease-GWAS study archetype and effect-size/structure signals favor PGS000903.

Both candidates are near-clones for the target (same trait_reported/trait_efo, same phenotyping_reported, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same basic covariates, same publication family) and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC differences (0.571 vs 0.572) are essentially noise. Tie-breakers favor PGS000613: it has a stronger top-1% vs rest OR (2.91 vs 1.47) and a better Brier score (0.0821 vs 0.0917), with slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.292) and more variants (15 vs 13). PGS000610’s only clear edge is a trivially higher full-model AUROC and pseudo-R², which are not decisive without PRS-only metrics.

PGS003586 has markedly better endpoint fidelity to the target trait: its phenotyping_reported is “Pre-eclampsia/eclampsia” and trait_reported is “Pre-eclampsia,” whereas PGS004593’s phenotyping_reported is “Gestational hypertension,” which is a related but non-identical hypertensive disorder of pregnancy and thus a weaker match for preeclampsia. Both candidates lack PRS-comparable AUC/R2, so effect-size and study context matter more; PGS003586 reports a stronger per-SD effect (OR 1.31) than PGS004593’s HR 1.16, suggesting more discriminative PRS signal. Additionally, PGS003586 comes from a clearly disease-focused multi-cohort Nat Med study with explicit training cohorts and a large stated training sample, while PGS004593 has N/A training size and no listed development cohorts, making its evidence package thinner despite larger evaluation N.

PGS001864 is the better-supported choice on endpoint fidelity and transportability: it targets the broad urolithiasis concept directly (trait_efo=urolithiasis; phenotyping_reported=Urinary calculus) and comes from a portability-focused evaluation with explicitly multi-ancestry EVAL (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS) and a large EUR training set. PGS001250, while closely related, is narrower/more packaged as a time-to-event endpoint (TTE calculus of kidney and ureter; trait_efo=ureterolithiasis, nephrolithiasis), and it is from the known pan-trait sparse UKB framework (“813 traits”), which domain guidance flags as less reliable for external transfer. Although PGS001250 reports clean PRS-only AUROC/R² (0.5668; 0.00592) and PGS001864 lacks PRS-only AUC/R² (only partial-r=0.0323), the framework penalty plus the TTE endpoint makes that metric advantage insufficient to outweigh PGS001864’s more direct disease framing and broader evaluation context.

PGS001795 is better-supported for uterine cancer risk prediction because it provides a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with ~912k variants, which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the 18-variant GWAS-hits score in PGS000541. Endpoint fidelity is acceptable for both (both phenotyping_reported are uterine cancer/uterus malignancy; EFOs are near-synonymous uterine cancer/carcinoma). PGS000541’s reported AUROC (0.576) is a full-model metric and not PRS-only, so it is less informative for ranking PRS quality despite having per-SD OR=1.311; overall, PGS001795 has stronger direct PRS evidence and model structure, even though it comes from a global biobank framework paper and has heavier basic covariates.

PGS001536 has a coherent vitiligo endpoint (trait_reported/phenotyping_reported both vitiligo, albeit time-to-event) and provides clean PRS-only performance metrics (PGS AUROC(no covariates)=0.64193; PGS R2=0.01621), with basic covariates only and a large, clearly described UKB development/validation setting plus some multi-ancestry evaluation. In contrast, PGS000738 has a major endpoint/metadata mismatch (phenotyping_reported="Red hair" despite vitiligo labels) and lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R2 (only a pseudo R²/full_model_r2=0.0386 and a beta), making its support for vitiligo prediction much less reliable on the visible fields.

Both candidates match the target endpoint well (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all indicate T2D) and neither reports clean PRS-only AUC/R2, so full-model AUROC is not a reliable cross-model PRS comparator. Given that, PGS002308 is better-supported: it comes from a disease-focused trans-ancestry PRS development/validation study (PRS-CSx) with explicitly diverse GWAS and evaluation ancestries and shows a stronger per-SD effect size (OR 1.96 vs 1.67 for PGS004152), which is a meaningful proxy for PRS discriminative strength when PRS-only metrics are absent. PGS004152 is from a multi-biobank methods evaluation/ensemble context with EUR-only GWAS and provides only full-model metrics (AUROC ~0.64) that are not directly comparable; its larger validation N does not outweigh the weaker effect-size signal and narrower GWAS ancestry context.

PGS002075 is the stronger pick on structural and transportability grounds: it uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2) with very large variant coverage (731,196) and comes from a portability-focused evaluation explicitly spanning multiple ancestries (AFR/EAS/EUR/GME/SAS), which is more consistent with robust PRS signal capture than the very sparse snpnet model in PGS001250 (341 variants) from the pan-trait “813 traits” framework paper. While PGS001250 has clean PRS-only metrics reported (PGS-only AUROC 0.5668; PGS-only R² 0.00592), its endpoint is time-to-event (“TTE calculus of kidney and ureter”), which is a mild endpoint mismatch for a generic urolithiasis target and can be less comparable; PGS002075’s phenotype is a direct diagnosis-style ‘Urinary calculus’ aligned to urolithiasis. However, confidence is low because PGS002075 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² and only reports a modest partial correlation (0.0385), making the empirical performance comparison against PGS001250 uncertain.

PGS000738 is better supported for the target trait vitiligo because its endpoint context is more directly disease-focused (publication explicitly about autoimmune vitiligo and polygenic inheritance), whereas PGS000760’s phenotyping_reported is a treatment-induced, therapy-specific outcome (“anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients”), which is a clear endpoint mismatch/packaging signal for generic vitiligo risk. Neither candidate reports PRS-only AUC/R2, so performance can’t be cleanly compared; however, PGS000738 at least provides a direct vitiligo evaluation with a pseudo R² (0.0386) and a larger validation sample (n=4,702 vs n=1,584). PGS000760 has a moderate HR (1.41) and large training N, but those do not compensate for the therapy-specific phenotype misalignment relative to vitiligo.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and neither provides a PRS-only AUC/R2, so we must lean on study archetype, structural signals, and available effect/performance evidence. PGS004253 is from a disease-focused UC study (immune checkpoint inhibitor–mediated colitis context but UC PRS) using a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,575) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR=1.84, 95% CI 1.76–1.93), which is a meaningful discriminator signal. Its reported AUROC=0.66 is full-model but uses only basic covariates (age/sex/array/PCs), so it is at least not obviously clinically packaged. In contrast, PGS001855 comes from a UKB portability framework paper (a known weaker archetype for external performance), is a sparse penalized-regression score with only 1,505 variants, and its only quantitative metric is a modest partial correlation (partial-r=0.0625) without an effect-size summary, offering weaker evidence of discriminative power despite larger training/validation and multi-ancestry evaluation. Overall, the disease-focused genome-wide model with strong OR support (PGS004253) is better-supported than the portability-framework sparse score (PGS001855).

Both candidates are near-clones: same trait/EFO and phenotyping (“Cancer of bladder”), same method (GWAS Hits) with the same 13 variants, same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL ancestry, same basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1–4), and same publication family—so differences are mostly noise-level. Candidate_b (PGS000610) has a trivially higher full-model AUROC (0.572 vs 0.567) and pseudo-R² (0.013 vs 0.0114), but these are not PRS-only metrics and the AUROC CIs overlap. Candidate_a (PGS000611) shows stronger risk stratification evidence (OR top 1% vs rest 2.66 vs 1.47) with tighter CI, and slightly larger training/validation samples (UKB n=12,992; eval n=13,530 vs MGI n=7,469; eval n=7,622), which modestly supports robustness. Given the lack of PRS-only AUC/R² for both, I weight the stronger effect-size/stratification signal and larger support toward PGS000611, but confidence is low due to high similarity and overlapping performance uncertainty.

Both candidates have clean endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all ulcerative colitis) and similarly basic covariates. PGS001306 has explicit PRS-only metrics (PGS-only AUROC 0.630, PGS-only R2 0.020) and broader evaluation ancestries, but it is from a known pan-trait UKB sparse-framework archetype (“across 813 traits”, snpnet, 179 variants) that domain guidance flags as often underperforming disease-focused scores in external validation. PGS004253 is disease-focused (UC PRS used to predict ICI-mediated colitis), uses a genome-wide shrinkage approach (LDpred2-auto) with very large variant coverage (744,575) and reports a strong per-SD effect size (OR 1.84), which is a strong PRS-quality signal even though only a full-model AUROC (0.66) is shown and PRS-only AUC/R2 are missing. Given the framework penalty and structural/effect-size strength, PGS004253 is more likely to rank higher, but confidence is low because PGS004253 lacks PRS-only performance metrics while PGS001306 provides them.

Both candidates are near-clones: same uterine cancer endpoint/phenotyping (“Malignant neoplasm of uterus”), same publication/family (Cancer PRSweb), same EUR-only GWAS/DEV/EVAL, same training cohort (UKB) and sizes, same basic covariates, and no PRS-only AUC/R2 reported (only full-model metrics). In this like-for-like setting, PGS000541 has slightly better overall discrimination metrics (full-model AUROC 0.576 vs 0.572; Nagelkerke R² 0.0133 vs 0.0126) and a marginally higher per-SD OR (1.311 vs 1.302), while PGS000542’s only edge is a higher top-1% OR (2.6 vs 2.12). Given the tiny metric differences and lack of PRS-only performance, the advantage is weak, hence low confidence, but PGS000541 is marginally better-supported overall.

PGS001795 is better-supported for uterine cancer because it provides a PRS-comparable metric (PGS-only / covariates-regressed-out Nagelkerke R2=0.001948) and uses a genome-wide shrinkage method (PRS-CS-auto) with ~912k variants, which is structurally more likely to capture polygenic signal than the very sparse P+T score in PGS000542 (20 variants). Both candidates have acceptable endpoint alignment (uterine cancer/uterine carcinoma vs malignant neoplasm of uterus) and EUR evaluation, but PGS000542 reports only full-model AUROC/R2 (AUROC=0.572) without PRS-only metrics, making its performance evidence less directly attributable to the PRS. PGS001795’s PRS-only R2 is also below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.0116), so it passes the sanity check. Framework-paper origin and heavier covariate set in PGS001795 temper confidence, but overall the combination of PRS-only metric evidence plus genome-wide construction outweighs PGS000542’s sparse model with only covariate-influenced metrics.

Both candidates are near-clones from the same publication (Cancer PRSweb), with identical endpoint alignment (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all bladder cancer), identical basic covariates (age, sex, batch, PCs 1-4), identical EUR-only training/validation context (UKB; EUR; same training n=12,992 and validation n=13,530), and neither reports PRS-only AUC/R2 (so full-model AUROC is only a within-family tie-break). Within this matched setting, PGS000613 shows consistently slightly stronger performance/effect evidence than PGS000611: higher full-model AUROC (0.571 vs 0.567), higher Nagelkerke R² (0.0125 vs 0.0114), higher top-1% OR (2.91 vs 2.66), and slightly higher per-SD OR (1.301 vs 1.284). Given the otherwise identical design, these aligned improvements favor PGS000613.

Both candidates match the target endpoint cleanly (trait_reported/trait_efo/phenotyping_reported all “Ulcerative colitis”) and both are UKB-derived framework-style scores with only basic covariates (no obvious clinical leakage). The key differentiator is that PGS001306 reports directly PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.63006; PGS-only R²=0.02036) with a European selected validation record, and its PRS-only R² is plausibly below the provided heritability ceiling (h2_liability≈0.2646), making the metric interpretable. PGS001855 lacks PRS-comparable AUC/R² entirely and only provides a partial correlation (0.0625), which is harder to benchmark against typical PRS discrimination and offers weaker direct evidence of standalone PRS performance despite larger training N and more variants. Therefore PGS001306 is better-supported on the visible fields.

PGS001536 is endpoint-faithful to vitiligo (trait_reported vitiligo; phenotyping_reported TTE vitiligo) and provides clean PRS-comparable performance (PGS-only AUROC=0.64193; PGS-only R2=0.01621), with basic covariates and a large validation (n=67,425) plus multi-ancestry evaluation context. Its PRS-only R2 is also well below the vitiligo heritability ceiling (h2_obs~0.17), making it plausible. In contrast, PGS000760 has a major phenotype mismatch: phenotyping_reported is anti-PD-L1 induced hypothyroidism in cancer patients (treatment-induced, different endpoint), with no PRS-comparable AUC/R2 and only an HR=1.41 from a small validation (n=1,584), making it much less supported for generic vitiligo risk prediction despite the vitiligo label fields.
